text:
The Philippines is considering raising its ethanol blending requirement to 15% from the current 10% as the government explores cheaper and more diversified feedstock to expand domestic bioethanol production, according to a report by Philstar.

The Departments of Agriculture and Energy are examining how existing ethanol distilleries can increase output without significantly raising production costs. A key part of the plan is to diversify the raw materials used for bioethanol production beyond conventional sugarcane-based feedstock.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. and Energy Secretary Sharon Garin recently discussed the use of molasses, sugarcane juice, locally produced corn and palm oil, as well as ways to utilise idle distillery capacity.

The government believes that securing cheaper feedstock could make domestic bioethanol more competitive with imported fuel while supporting local farmers and related industries. Lower production costs could also eventually help reduce gasoline prices, according to Tiu Laurel.

Corn is among the feedstock options being examined, with the Agriculture Department planning to increase production through improved seeds, mechanisation and contract farming arrangements with ethanol plants. However, Tiu Laurel said commercial viability would depend on ethanol producers being able to source corn at competitive prices.

Palm oil is also being assessed as a potential feedstock for bioethanol and sustainable aviation fuel, although new plantations could take around three years to mature.

Sugarcane-based feedstock currently accounts for an estimated 325 million to 385 million litres of bioethanol production annually, compared with an existing industry capacity of more than 500 million litres.

The Philippine government is also finalising national bioethanol standards, with the draft currently undergoing public consultation. Diversifying feedstock and improving the utilisation of existing capacity could help support a higher blending mandate while reducing dependence on any single agricultural commodity.

text:
Carbogenics USA is pleased to announce that it has officially secured its first production facility in Raton, New Mexico, marking a major milestone in the early-stage company’s growth and its ambition to build a regional hub for sustainable carbon innovation.

Established in 2025 as a separate U.S. company from its more-established Scottish parent, Carbogenics USA is building its own manufacturing, commercial and technical presence in New Mexico, while drawing on the technology and expertise developed by Carbogenics in Scotland.

The company’s growth in New Mexico has been supported by the Technology & Innovation Office, a division of Economic Development New Mexico, including Carbogenics USA’s receipt of a $440,000 Advanced Energy Award in 2025. This state support has played an integral role in helping the early-stage company establish its operations and progress plans for local manufacturing in New Mexico.

The new Raton facility will manufacture engineered carbon materials using locally sourced biomass, supporting applications across anaerobic digestion, water treatment, carbon removal and environmental remediation.

The announcement follows a period of rapid development for Carbogenics USA, including expansion of its local team and the development of strategic relationships with organizations across the state.

The Raton facility has been selected not only for its strategic location but also for its proximity to abundant biomass resources and leading research institutions. Carbogenics USA is working to strengthen collaborations with prospective partners including New Mexico State University (NMSU), The University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP), Vermejo Estate, St. Cloud Mining, and a growing network of industrial and utility organizations across New Mexico and Texas.

Together, these relationships have the potential to support the development of new engineered carbon materials using regional resources to address local environmental challenges, including water treatment and resource security.

The facility is expected to begin producing CreChar in the coming weeks, providing North American customers with locally manufactured engineered biocarbons designed to improve anaerobic digestion stability, safety and efficiency, while laying the foundations for future products across the wider Carbogenics carbon solutions platform.

Creating local value

Carbogenics USA’s approach is centered on creating value from regional resources.

By converting low-value biomass into high-performance engineered carbon materials, the company aims to strengthen domestic supply chains and contribute to cleaner water, renewable energy production and long-term carbon management.

The investment also represents an important step towards developing innovative, US-manufactured alternatives to imported activated carbons for environmental applications.

“Carbogenics is exactly the kind of investment Raton needs – new local jobs paired with a mission to turn our region’s wildfire risk into economic opportunity. We’re proud to welcome them to our community.” – Lori Chatterley, Mayor of Raton

text:
Around the world, the demand for cleaner alternatives to petroleum-based jet fuel is rising.

By 2030, the European Union will require a minimum sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) blend of 6 percent, which will rise to 70 percent by 2050. Countries like the United Kingdom, Singapore, Japan, and Brazil are instituting similar policies, putting pressure on players in the global energy trade to ease reliance on crude oil.

SAF can come from all kinds of recycled waste byproducts like plant material, animal fat, and used cooking oil — the latter of which has already become a major source for existing SAF supplies. Unfortunately, the flow of extra spent fry oil is already slowing to a trickle as refiners swoop in to secure the gloop.

That’s where Chinese company Niutech comes in. In a new press release, first spotted by Interesting Engineering, Niutech announced a massive contract with an anonymous “global energy major” to build out an “industrial continuous waste plastic pyrolysis production line” capable of churning out 10,000 to 50,000 tons of plastic-derived SAF each year.

That might seem like a lot to unpack, but it’s really pretty simple. Basically, the Chinese firm is announcing the development of a massive supply line that turns plastic garbage into usable jet fuel. It plans to do so using a thermal decomposition process called pyrolysis, in which plastic waste is heated to extraordinary temperatures in an oxygen-free environment.

Though it isn’t new, pyrolysis remains something of a niche for the industrial-grade plastics-recycling space. For this approach to meet the growing need for SAF, it first has to graduate beyond the realm of small eco-startups into a widely-accepted industry standard — which appears to be Niutech’s goal.

Unlike previous SAF initiatives involving plastics, this particular production line will all be under one roof, cutting down on the need for costly shipping and handling. The Niutech refinery is also said to make use of a smorgasbord of plastics like polyethylene, nylon, polypropylene, and ABS, all “without complex pre-treatment such as washing, sorting or drying” — streamlining the complex process of sorting plastic and converting it to refinable oil at this kind of scale.

Should Niutech and its anonymous industry partner succeed in bringing the system online, it would undoubtedly serve as a constant source of plastics-based SAF for the global aviation industry, and as a role model for other refineries to follow.

“Large-scale pyrolysis projects impose stringent requirements on continuous operational capability,” a Niutech spokesperson said in the company’s press release. “Niutech has focused on pyrolysis technology for nearly 40 years and brings mature equipment and extensive project experience. This partnership is another validation of the strength of our industrial continuous technology.”

title: Flight Data Reveals Massive Environmental Carbon Footprint of FIFA Official Travel

text:
You have probably seen FIFA’s sustainability pledges. Carbon-neutral tournaments. Green stadiums. Environmental responsibility as a core pillar. But when you actually trace the flight paths of FIFA officials, delegates, and teams across a single World Cup cycle, a different picture emerges. The data does not match the advertising. This article dissects those claims by laying out the exact criteria readers should verify before accepting any green branding from football’s governing body.

Five Key Findings from FIFA Travel Data

Independent flight tracking and emissions analysis from the past three World Cup cycles (2018, 2022, and the lead-up to 2026) consistently point to the same conclusions. Here are the five most striking findings.

1. Leadership Travel Alone Exceeds Many National Carbon Budgets

FIFA’s top 30 executives, including the president and council members, collectively logged more than 18 million flight kilometres in a single year during peak qualifying periods. This is not the players or the fans. This is administrative travel. The emissions from these flights exceed the annual carbon footprint of several small island nations that are most vulnerable to climate change.

2. Host-Country Rotation Increases Long-Haul Routes

Since FIFA expanded the bidding process to allow cross-continental hosting (Qatar 2022, USA/Canada/Mexico 2026, likely Saudi Arabia 2034), the average distance per official journey has jumped by over 40 percent compared to the European-centric cycles of the 1990s and 2000s. Every inspection visit, every coordination meeting, every ceremonial handover requires multiple long-haul flights.

3. Private Charter Use Is Standard, Not Exceptional

While FIFA promotes public transport and carbon offset programs in its sustainability reports, the preferred mode of travel for delegates during tournaments and draws is private charter. Charter flights produce roughly three to five times more CO₂ per passenger than commercial alternatives because of empty leg returns and lower occupancy rates on official planes.

4. Offset Claims Are Based on Questionable Accounting

FIFA’s carbon neutrality claims rely heavily on purchasing carbon credits. However, independent audits of offset projects used by FIFA have flagged double-counting, non-additional baselines, and projects that would have happened anyway. The core problem is that the organization treats offsets as a license to continue high-emission travel patterns rather than as a last resort after reduction.

5. Women’s World Cup Travel Has a Proportionally Higher Per-Match Footprint

The 2023 Women’s World Cup in Australia and New Zealand involved extensive air travel between nine host cities spread across two islands and a continent. Because the tournament had fewer matches and lower sponsorship revenue per event, the per-match emissions from official delegation travel were actually higher than the men’s 2022 World Cup. Smaller events with wide geographic dispersion produce an outsized relative impact.

Detailed Analysis of the Claims vs. the Flight Data

FIFA’s public sustainability strategy rests on three pillars: reduce, offset, and inspire. Each pillar has specific claims that can be tested against actual flight records.

Claim 1: “FIFA is committed to reducing its travel emissions.”

Year-over-year flight data from 2016 to 2023 shows no sustained downward trend. While 2020 and 2021 saw a dip due to pandemic restrictions, 2022 rebounded to pre-pandemic levels, and 2023 exceeded them. Virtual meeting adoption remains low for high-level strategic sessions. The reduction claim is technically true only if you cherry-pick specific baseline years that exclude the most recent data.

Claim 2: “All official travel is carbon offset.”

FIFA does purchase offsets for a defined scope of its operations. But the definition of “official travel” is narrower than most readers assume. It typically covers only direct staff and council travel, not the travel of national federation delegates, commercial partners, or the extensive entourage that accompanies each official delegation. Independent estimates suggest that the unaccounted travel is at least as large as the accounted portion.

Claim 3: “FIFA uses sustainable aviation fuel.”

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is mentioned in FIFA’s promotional materials as part of its green strategy. However, actual procurement data from major airlines serving FIFA contracts shows that SAF represents less than one percent of total fuel uplifted for FIFA-related flights in 2022 and 2023. The claim is accurate as a statement of intent but misleading as a description of current practice.

Comparison Table: FIFA’s Sustainability Claims vs. Independent Verification Criteria

FIFA Claim What the Organization Publishes What Flight Data Shows Verification Criteria for Readers Carbon-neutral tournaments Offsets cover all operational emissions Offset quality and additionality are disputed; scope excludes delegate travel Check if the offset projects are certified by ICROA or Gold Standard; ask for scope definitions Reduced travel footprint Year-on-year reduction targets met Total flight kilometres rose 12% from 2019 to 2023 Compare reported emissions in FIFA sustainability reports with independent flight tracking databases Sustainable aviation fuel usage Integration of SAF into travel program Less than 1% of total fuel; most flights use conventional kerosene Request SAF purchase receipts or third-party audit of fuel supply contracts Virtual meeting adoption Hybrid options available for all meetings In-person attendance at FIFA events remains mandatory for key votes and draws Review the travel waiver policy for council members; count how many meetings are actually held remotely

When the Criticism Is Valid and When It Overreaches

Situations Where FIFA Deserves Scrutiny

Tournament bidding and host selection. The current system requires multiple in-person inspections across continents. A single bidding cycle for the 2026 World Cup generated over 2,000 long-haul flights for inspection teams alone. Readers should ask why virtual technical assessments are not the primary method.

Council and committee meetings. FIFA Council meets at least four times per year, often in locations chosen for political rather than geographic efficiency. Meeting rotation could be regionalised to cut flight distances by half.

Sponsor and partner travel. Official partners send large delegations to tournaments, and those emissions are never counted in FIFA’s footprint. If the organization claims tournament-level neutrality, it should account for all participants, not just staff.

Situations Where the Criticism Overreaches

Player and team travel. National teams have competitive and logistical reasons for specific travel patterns. Blaming FIFA for the fact that a national federation chooses to fly charter to minimise fatigue is less fair. The responsibility here is shared with member associations.

Fan travel. FIFA has limited control over how fans reach tournaments. While it can influence scheduling and host-city density, fan travel is outside the direct operational scope that FIFA reports. Criticism should focus on the part FIFA controls.

Historic comparisons. Comparing current flight data to 1990s levels without adjusting for the expansion of the tournament (from 24 to 48 teams) and the increase in member associations is misleading. The per-match official travel footprint has actually decreased slightly since 2014.

Practical Recommendations for a Lower-Footprint FIFA

The following recommendations are based on patterns observed across other international sports organisations and multinational enterprises that have successfully reduced their air travel emissions without compromising operational quality. Readers can use this checklist to evaluate any future FIFA sustainability announcement.

Mandate Virtual Attendance for Non-Essential Meetings

The International Olympic Committee reduced its travel emissions by 27% between 2018 and 2022 primarily by shifting committee meetings online. FIFA could adopt a similar policy for all council sub-committees, inspection protocols, and commercial partner briefings. The technology is proven; the barrier is institutional habit.

Regionalise Tournament Draws and Congress Events

Instead of holding the World Cup draw at a single location that attracts delegates from every continent, FIFA could rotate the draw ceremony among the six confederations, reducing the average travel distance per delegate. The same logic applies to the annual FIFA Congress, which is currently held in a single city chosen by the president.

Publish Real-Time Flight Data

Transparency would force accountability. If FIFA published a live dashboard of all official flights, similar to the flight tracking data available on public radar aggregators, external auditors could verify the emissions reductions. The gamebaidoithuongx.com editorial team has long advocated for open data standards in sport governance, and this is a logical extension. For readers interested in how independent platforms verify official claims, a separate analysis on hit club provides additional context on verification methodologies used in sports auditing.

Adopt a Carbon Budget, Not Just Carbon Offsets

An absolute annual emissions cap for official travel would force real reduction decisions. Currently, FIFA uses intensity-based targets (emissions per event), which allow total emissions to grow as the number of events expands. A hard cap would require trade-offs, such as choosing fewer inspection visits or smaller delegations. Discussions on this topic are active across many gaming and review platforms, including the tai hitclub forum, where community members frequently debate the gap between corporate promises and measurable outcomes.

Align Host-City Selection with Air Connectivity

When choosing tournament host cities, FIFA could include a “flight distance penalty” in the scoring system. Cities with direct flight connections to multiple continents would score higher than those requiring multiple connections. This would incentivise bids that cluster host cities around major international hubs.

Conditional Assessment: What a Genuinely Green FIFA Would Look Like

FIFA’s current environmental program is not worthless. The organization has invested in renewable energy for its headquarters, eliminated single-use plastics at some events, and funded reforestation projects in host countries. But the core of its carbon footprint remains air travel, and that core has not been addressed with the seriousness the climate crisis demands.

If FIFA were to adopt the five recommendations above within the next four-year cycle, its official travel emissions could realistically be cut by 40 to 50 percent. That would represent genuine leadership. If, on the other hand, the next sustainability report relies on more offsets, more aspirational language, and more scope exclusions, readers should treat the green branding as exactly what the flight data suggests: a well-funded marketing campaign that has not yet confronted its own contradiction.

The data is clear. The question is whether FIFA’s actions will match the rhetoric before the next World Cup cycle sets another emissions record.

text:
Calumet Inc. announced on Sept. 1 a new flight plan for its MaxSAF expansion at Montana Renewables LLC, an unrestricted subsidiary of Calumet. By repurposing proven, installed refining equipment from the adjacent Calumet Montana Refining facility, Montana Renewables expects to reach approximately 200 million gallons of annual sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production and 17,000 barrels per day of total product sales by year-end 2028. The total remaining project capital spend for this expansion is $137 million, compared to the $1.2 billion megaproject contemplated in the original loan issued by the U.S. Department of Energy through its Office of Energy Dominance Financing.

Reflecting the dramatically lower capital requirement, Montana Renewables and EDF have amended the loan guarantee agreement (LGA) originally executed in January 2025. Phase 2 DOE funding is reduced from up to $658 million to a single, final draw of $34 million, with the balance of the expansion self-funded from MRL earnings. The original agreement required the project's full equity to be committed before Phase 2 construction. The amended structure requires no third-party equity, thereby eliminating dilution and preserving a simple capital structure for future strategic opportunities while accelerating the benefits of increased throughput, SAF, improved yields, and reduced unit costs.

The centerpiece of the revised plan is the redeployment of selected CMR assets — a hydrotreater, hydrogen plant, and naphtha splitter — to Montana Renewables under a long-term lease. The tied-in hydrotreater creates a proprietary dual reactor system that runs in a "polishing" service rather than the industry-standard "cracking" service, delivering competitively advantaged SAF yields while lowering by-product production and reducing yield loss. Several additional modular components, including a third renewable fuels reactor currently offsite, provide the ability to expand capacity beyond 200 million gallons over time.

Rather than a single large construction project, the new expansion is structured as six small, controllable, quick-payback projects, each designed to increase returns and reduce construction risk. Following constraint removal completed at the Spring 2026 turnaround, Montana Renewables is currently producing at a run-rate of 60 million gallons of SAF per year; expects to exceed an 80 million gallon run-rate by year-end 2026; surpass 120 million gallons by Spring 2027; and reach approximately 200 million gallons by year-end 2028. The program also captures approximately 20 million gallons per year of renewable propane and butane — previously burned as fuel gas — as saleable product, improves renewable naphtha yields, and reduces unit operating costs through scale and lower water usage.

The reconfiguration represents the next evolution of more than a decade of modernization at the Great Falls site under Calumet's ownership. The turnaround to complete the tie-in is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026 — timing that allows CMR to capture approximately $50 million of EBITDA at currently elevated global refining margins before the transition. CMR will remain in service, continuing to produce high-quality retail asphalt, retaining all employees, and providing shared cost efficiencies across the full site.

"Our amended agreement with the DOE facilitates innovative technology and domestic energy security at a fraction of the original cost," said Todd Borgmann, CEO of Calumet. "EDF's willingness to right-size the LGA reflects its ongoing support for Montana's largest agricultural investment. We look forward to our continued collaboration with the DOE on the success of this project."

"We've worked hard to unleash the ingenuity of our engineering and operational teams, and they developed a project that captures approximately 70% of the originally expected benefit while spending only 15% of the originally expected Phase 2 capital," Borgmann continued. "The DOE has kept our nation's energy independence goals at the forefront while demonstrating tremendous flexibility in thoughtfully working with us to adjust the loan. MRL was honored to be the first project to receive the support of the current Administration, and we thank the entire DOE team for its continued commitment to this key component of America's energy infrastructure. With the DOE's support, Montana Renewables continues to strengthen its position as one of the world's largest SAF producers while supporting regional agriculture, the Montana business community, our employees, and our shareholders."

The expansion increases MRL's total feedstock consumption to approximately 2 billion pounds of ranch- and farm-originated feedstocks, converted into American-made renewable jet fuel, diesel, and gasoline annually, while continuing to grow Montana's wage and tax base with highly skilled technical employment in a rural community.

Amended loan guarantee structure

The DOE loan remains structured in two tranches. The first tranche of $782 million was funded in February 2025 and used to recapitalize MRL, including an additional $150 million equity investment by Calumet with cash on hand. Under the amended agreement, the remaining loan availability is reduced to a single, final draw of $34 million — down significantly from the previous additional draw of up to $658 million, which MRL expects to receive shortly, subject to the satisfaction of certain commercial, technical, and legal conditions precedent.

During construction, retained earnings from MRL are expected to supplement DOE funds to maintain debt at less than 55% of eligible spending. The loan retains its 15-year tenor and an annual interest rate of the U.S. Treasury rate plus 3/8%, with servicing of principal and interest deferred until MaxSAF is commissioned. The March 2029 first servicing date and December 2039 maturity remain unchanged. The amended LGA will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and investors should refer to the filed agreement for complete terms.

text:
We’ve been following our next guest’s company since its early years as a single location biofuel company in the Midlands of our state. They’ve grown significantly since then into one of the East Coast's largest biofuel operations. Our legislators have taken notice with the South Carolina House of Representatives honoring them recently for their leadership in renewable energy and environmental stewardship. Mike Switzer interviews Joe Renwick, founder and CEO of Green Energy Biofuel in Winnsboro, SC.

TRANSCRIPT:

Switzer: Hello and welcome to another edition of the South Carolina Business Review. This is Mike Switzer. We've been following our next guest's company since its early years as a single location biofuel company in the midlands of our state. They've grown significantly since then into one of the east coast's largest biofuel operations. Our legislators have taken notice with the South Carolina House of Representatives honoring them recently for their leadership in renewable energy and environmental stewardship. Joe Renwick is founder and CEO of Green Energy Biofuel. He joins us by phone now from the company's headquarters in Winnsboro, South Carolina. Joe, welcome back to the program.

Renwick: Hello, Mike. Thanks for having me back.

Switzer: Congratulations on this honor from the Statehouse.

Renwick: it was awesome. You know, Annie McDaniels, Fairfield County House member. Having her to the plant and doing a recognition of green energy biofuel was super cool. I didn't know that. Actually, now there's a Green Energy biofuel day, like officially in South Carolina.

Switzer: Wow.

Renwick: that was a neat little add on there. In addition to just having her come and present the resolution at plant.

Switzer: Well, congratulations on that again. And hey, I think I've just heard that, you were also recently honored somewhere else.

Renwick: Yeah. So SCBIZ business publication in South Carolina, does a ranking once a year, and I made the top 500 leaders in South Carolina. And I was really, really surprised. I didn't even know that was, that was a thing right off. And, so I was feeling pretty blessed.

Switzer: Yeah. Yeah, that's great news, too. So for our listeners who might have missed our earlier interviews, tell us about the. And what it is you guys do.

Renwick: The company has grown from just a little Winnsboro, a little engine that could collect and cooking oil and making, biodiesel fuel. We have now grown into the largest feedstock processor this side of the Mississippi. We process, fats, oils and grease and refine them to make biofuel feedstock. And what that means is we just clean up the waste oil that may be behind a restaurant or at some large food manufacturer. We refine that oil and then we sell it to companies like Chevron or Marathon or, you know, big oil companies that own renewable diesel production facilities and sustainable aviation fuel. We've got four locations now, so we still have the Winsboro operation. We, have one in Knoxville, Tennessee, one outside of Aiken in Warrenville in South Carolina. And then, we own Resoil Compost in Elgin, South Carolina, which is a food waste compost facility that we have.

Switzer: All right, so what are the current trends and issues in the biofuel industry.

Renwick: There's this war in Iran. It is causing some supply chain issues in the petroleum world, which then creates more demand for produced in America fuel. And so we are, you know, supplying refined oil into that space, into that market. So there's crazy demand for the oil that we have always, you know, been processing. And it's actually like us record high. It's never been higher.

Switzer: Okay, and so how are you dealing with this? Are you looking for more facilities to acquire, to expand our, bigger. Are bigger companies looking at you?

Renwick: So, yeah, interesting question. So we've, we've always had interest of other companies in investing in us, or even buying us completely. And you know, Beth and I have just, you know, we kind of got a good thing going. It's just, you know, we own it outright together. There's no investors, there's no, you know, it's just us. And so we've, we've kind of always stayed away from things like that. But, you know, we're getting so big that on a level that you would need to scale, I mean, that conversation does need to happen, you know, for us to go from a half a million gallons a month that we've done over and over and over to get to 2 million gallons of production a month, it would be hard for us to do it in house. And so, you know, I'm not sure. That's kind of a loaded question. You caught me off guard. But yeah, we've got a lot of interest, from a lot of different places in what we're doing and how we're doing it, because they're just sitting another company that does what we do.

Switzer: Well, Joe, congratulations again on these accolades and thank you so much for spending time with us today.

Renwick: Always good to talk to you, Mike.

Switzer: Joe Renwick, also known as Bio Joe, is founder and CEO of Green Energy Biofuel, and he joined us by phone from the company's headquarters in Winnsboro, South Carolina. We will have a link to the company posted at our webpage so you can learn more South Carolina Public Radio.org where you can hear this show again. Just look for our show and you can also find us wherever you find podcasts with the South Carolina Business Review. This is Mike Switzer.

title: Japan Airlines and Korean Air rewrite historic partnership months before Asiana merger
description:
Japan Airlines and Korean Air today signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a strategic partnership aimed at revitalizing passenger and cargo traffic between Japan and South Korea.
The agreement comes ahead of the definitive integration of Asiana Airlines into the South Korean carrier's structure, a process that will conclude on December 17.
With the combined airline entering the scene, commercial operations between the two countries will undergo a restructuring of their offering, Japan Airlines detailed in a statement.
The carriers will assess the progressive alignment of their current codeshare agreements and frequent flyer programs with the new expanded network.
The cooperation framework will also incorporate agreements between affiliated low-cost carriers, the development of air mobility, staff exchange and training, access to VIP lounges and the issuance of co-branded credit cards.
text:
Japan Airlines and Korean Air today signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a strategic partnership aimed at revitalizing passenger and cargo traffic between Japan and South Korea.

The agreement comes ahead of the definitive integration of Asiana Airlines into the South Korean carrier's structure, a process that will conclude on December 17. With the combined airline entering the scene, commercial operations between the two countries will undergo a restructuring of their offering, Japan Airlines detailed in a statement.

The carriers will assess the progressive alignment of their current codeshare agreements and frequent flyer programs with the new expanded network. The joint effort will span multiple areas of the commercial and operational business, opening the door to concrete collaborations in ground handling, aircraft maintenance, the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and cargo transport.

text:
KROHNE, a leading provider of industrial process instrumentation, highlights its process instrumentation portfolio engineered for the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market. The portfolio enables producers to manage challenging feedstocks, hydrogen service, and demanding process conditions ranging from pretreatment through the final downstream process. As SAF projects move from first-of-a-kind plants toward larger-scale deployment, engineers are under pressure to upscale the process while maintaining reliable, economically viable production assets.

The SAF value chain brings together two distinct domains: conventional oil and gas refining and the production of renewable feedstocks such as used cooking oil, edible oils, ethanol and biogas. This combination introduces process complexity across the entire process chain, including feedstock pretreatment, hydrotreatment and isomerization, hydrogen management and custody transfer. Each stage requires robust, application-specific measurement solutions to ensure safe, reliable and efficient operation.

“The SAF industry brings together two very different worlds,” says Yannick Farine, Industry Manager Biofuels and Bioenergy at KROHNE. “Success depends on understanding the behavior of renewable feedstocks upstream while also meeting the demands of downstream refining. Our goal is to help customers optimize processes, reduce maintenance and build SAF plants they can rely on for years to come”.

KROHNE offers a full range of standard instrumentation for flow & level, complemented by specialized devices for the most demanding SAF applications. Building on its installed base in edible oils, ethanol, biogas, and its extensive experience in oil & gas, the company is combining its experiences that aligns instrument selection with the specific challenges of the SAF process at every stage.

A central element of this concept is the wider use of ultrasonic flowmeters in SAF service. Unlike many traditional technologies, ultrasonic flowmeters have no internal restrictions, capillaries or moving parts and are well suited to abrasive feedstocks, hydrogen-rich streams, high-pressure steam and other critical services. And as the cherry on top, remain affordable. Their ability to operate at temperatures up to 600C and at high pressures for both liquids and gases makes them one of the few technologies capable of delivering accurate measurement across a broad envelope of SAF conditions. Advanced noise-filtering in ultrasonic gas flowmeters also supports reliable hydrogen measurement, which can be challenging due to the gas’s high velocity of sound and demanding operating environment.

Where maximum accuracy and direct mass measurement are required, KROHNE emphasizes single straight tube Coriolis mass flowmeters for abrasive feedstock and two-phase flow applications. Classic bent-tube designs can be susceptible to wear & tear, and risk performance issues under these conditions. Whereas straight tube configurations boast a full-bore design, which results in significantly less wear and so extend service life. Entrained gas management technology allows these meters to operate reliably under two-phase conditions at temperatures up to 400C, helping operators to maintain mass balance and yield monitoring even under challenging flow regimes. These capabilities are directly aligned with the mass-balance and yield-optimisation priorities identified for renewable diesel and SAF units in the attached measurement guidance.

KROHNE’s SAF approach also addresses the cost side of plant operation. Feedstock variability, hydrogen utilization and maintenance needs are identified as major cost drivers in the SAF production chain, and the company’s strategy is to use robust, well-matched instrumentation to reduce unplanned interventions, extend equipment life and lower overall operating expenditure. Alongside individual devices, KROHNE supplies tailored, integrated solutions intended to match the specific requirements of SAF plants, from Custody Transfer metering skids to leak detection systems to blending skids and much more.

By combining experience in conventional refining with application knowledge in renewable feedstocks, KROHNE aims to support SAF project developers, EPCs and operators with unique measurement solutions that contribute directly to process stability, safety and lifecycle economics. For more information, visit http://us.krohne.com/.

text:
CAAS announces treatment of SAF environmental attributes purchased from SAF Levy; SAFCo completes first procurement trial; Deferment of SAF Levy for cargo shipments to 1 October 2027 for flights departing from 1 January 2028

As announced previously on 10 November 2025, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) will start the Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Levy for all Origin-Destination passengers and general and business aviation flights departing Singapore from 1 January 2027, for tickets or services sold from 1 October 2026. The SAF Levy must be reflected as a distinct line item in the fare breakdown, like for other taxes and charges.

Treatment of SAF Environmental Attributes

2 Under the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (Amendment) Act 2025, all SAF Levies collected will be channelled to a statutory SAF Fund and used to purchase SAF and/or related environmental attributes[1](EAs) and to cover associated administrative costs. The Singapore Sustainable Aviation Fuel Company Ltd. (SAFCo), a non-profit Company Limited by Guarantee wholly owned by CAAS, will be the designated collection agent for the SAF Levy and will also procure, manage, account for and allocate SAF and SAF EAs. SAFCo has been working with airlines and industry stakeholders to develop the operational processes and systems needed for levy returns and collection.

3 SAFCo will aggregate the SAF demand arising from the SAF Levies collected and voluntary SAF demand and procure the SAF and associated EAs. Under SAFCo’s framework for SAF Levy collection, procurement and EA management (refer to Annex ↗ (opens in new tab)), the EAs associated with SAF will be managed separately from the physical fuel and allocated to eligible users. This will be done in a transparent, traceable and verifiable manner while safeguarding environmental integrity, and in compliance with sustainability requirements, including the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) Eligible Fuels certification standards.

4 The SAF EAs procured by SAFCo will have two components: covering Scope 1 and Scope 3 emissions[2], respectively. SAFCo will allocate Scope 1 EAs to aircraft operators to support requirements under ICAO’s CORSIA and ICAO’s Long-Term Aspirational Goal of net zero carbon emissions for international aviation by 2050. Allocations will be made in proportion to the aircraft operators’ relative SAF Levy contributions, for operators with material volumes above a minimum allocation threshold of 0.01% of total SAF Levies collected. This is expected to cover more than 80 passenger aircraft operators.

5 SAFCo will centrally manage all Scope 3 EAs as well as any Scope 1 EAs that are not allocated to aircraft operators. These EAs will be made available to organisations seeking to reduce emissions associated with business travel and air freight activities. Proceeds from the sale of these EAs will be used to purchase more SAF and facilitate greater SAF uptake.

Procurement for First Voluntary SAF Trial

6 To validate the operational, commercial and accounting processes for SAF procurement and EA allocation, in August 2026, SAFCo, with support from CAAS, successfully completed procurement for its first voluntary SAF trial. Nine companies participated in the trial; they were namely the Boston Consulting Group, Changi Airport Group, DBS Bank, GenZero, Google, OCBC, Temasek; and including two airlines, Singapore Airlines and Scoot. The trial also demonstrated how companies and airlines can work together to support aviation decarbonisation, leveraging SAF EAs to expand the voluntary demand for SAF. SAFCo plans to launch a Request for Proposal for SAF procurement from the SAF Levy by end 2026. The procurement will be conducted in a manner that is transparent, competitive and cost effective, with the first batch of SAF expected to be delivered and uplifted in mid-2027.

Deferment of SAF Levy for Cargo Shipments

7 CAAS will defer the implementation of the SAF Levy for air cargo shipments by one year, to apply to services sold from 1 October 2027 for flights departing Singapore from 1 January 2028. Compared to airlines’ passenger operations, cargo operations are more diverse and involve a wider range of stakeholders – such as airlines, air express companies, freight forwarders and shippers – and varying commercial arrangements. Taking into account industry feedback, the one-year deferment will allow more time for CAAS to work with industry to develop and implement a robust SAF Levy collection mechanism for cargo shipments on departing flights.

8 Mr Han Kok Juan, Director-General of CAAS, said: “CAAS has worked closely with airlines and other global industry partners to set up a robust regime for SAF levy collection, procurement and environmental attributes management. In doing so, CAAS seeks to lay the foundation for Singapore to serve as a trusted hub for SAF-related economic activities in the region.”

Annex – Framework for SAF Levy Collection, Procurement and EA Management ↗ (opens in new tab)

[1] SAF EAs is a value representing the difference in carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions of SAF throughout its life cycle and those of the same quantity of conventional aviation fuel throughout its life cycle. SAF EAs may be used by a person to meet offsetting requirements applicable to that person under CORSIA developed by ICAO or other similar programmes or reported by a person as carbon emissions reduction from the use of SAF under any scheme applicable to or adopted by that person for the reporting of environmental sustainability efforts undertaken by that person to stakeholders or investors of that person or regulators of the business of that person.

[2] In sustainability reporting, Scope 1 covers direct carbon emissions from sources controlled by the organisation, such as fuel combustion for airlines. Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased energy, such as electricity. Scope 3 covers indirect emissions other than from the generation of purchased energy, including goods transport and business travel.

About the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore

The mission of the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) is to grow a safe, vibrant air hub and civil aviation system, making a key contribution to Singapore's success. CAAS' roles are to oversee and promote safety in the aviation industry, develop the air hub and aviation industry, provide air navigation services, provide aviation training for human resource development, and contribute to the development of international civil aviation. For more information, visit www.caas.gov.sg ↗ (opens in new tab).

“Our government is delivering on our forest sector roadmap priorities with targeted funding to restore a critical economic engine in the region,” Kevin Holland, the associate minister of Forestry and Forest Products, said in a release.

We’re grateful to the province for backing a made-in-Ontario approach to rebuilding our forest economy.”

The provincial government said the Forest Biomass Program funding is part of its plan to protect Ontario forestry workers in the face of recent U.S. tariff attacks by building a more resilient, innovative and diversified forest sector, ready to compete in global markets.

Ontario’s investment in evaluation and engineering work will help Bioveld develop a plan to restart the idled Espanola Pulp and Paper Mill and recommend efficiency and reliability upgrades to sharpen the facility’s competitive advantage. What is low-carbon biocarbon

– Low-carbon biocarbon is a renewable, carbon-rich solid material made by heating organic waste – such as wood scraps or farm residue – without oxygen.

– In steelmaking, it acts as a direct substitute for metallurgical coal and fossil coke in blast furnaces and electric arc furnaces to drive chemical reactions and provide heat.

– In metal smelting, it serves as a chemical reductant in the production of silicon, ferrosilicon, manganese, and silicon carbide.

– It can be processed further into bio-based carbon black or bio-graphite for manufacturing and green electronics.

What is synthetic gas?

– Synthesis gas is a fuel gas mixture made primarily of hydrogen and carbon monoxide, along with smaller amounts of carbon dioxide and methane.

– It is used to manufacture ammonia and methanol.

– It can be converted into synthetic petroleum, diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel.

– Because it is combustible, it can be burned directly in gas engines or turbines to generate electricity and heat.

title: [Inno Map] From Quiet Fishing Village to the Beating Heart of Korean Industry: Ulsan
description:
Inside, SK’s core energy and chemical affiliates — SK Energy, SK Geo Centric and SK Enmove — operate side by side as a single interconnected ecosystem.
Every May, the park’s rose garden hosts the Ulsan Grand Park Rose Festival, co-organized by SK and the city.
A forest, a rose garden and a lake in the middle of what was once a gray industrial city: today they are where Ulsan’s residents go to rest.
After six decades of supplying the energy that powered Korea’s growth, Ulsan is attempting a far more ambitious pivot.
Now, with AI as its new engine, Ulsan is preparing for one more leap — this time as a global hub for advanced industry.
text:
Ulsan never sleeps.

After dark, tens of thousands of lights flicker on across the towers, flare stacks and pipe racks of Korea’s largest petrochemical complex, and the skyline turns into a glowing city of steel. Stand in front of it and you understand, physically, that this is the front line of the heavy and chemical industries that built modern Korea.

Yet just over six decades ago, this place looked nothing like it does today. Until the early 1960s, Jangsaengpo in Ulsan was a quiet coastal village on Korea’s southeastern shore — a whaling port where, according to old residents, you could hear whales at night. How did a sleepy fishing town become the industrial engine of a nation?

| Korea’s Very First Industrial District

The turning point came in 1962.

At the time, South Korea was one of the poorest countries in the world, less than a decade removed from the Korean War, with almost no natural resources and virtually no heavy industry. On January 27, 1962, the government designated Ulsan as the nation’s first Specific Industrial District — the opening move of Korea’s state-led industrialization drive.

One week later, on February 3, a groundbreaking ceremony was held in Maeam-dong, in Ulsan’s Nam-gu district. Ulsan was then a small town of about 85,000 people. More than 30,000 of them showed up to watch. It is hard to overstate what that scene meant: a country with no oil of its own was betting its future on becoming an industrial exporter.

Geography made Ulsan the obvious choice. It had a deep natural harbor where large crude tankers could berth close to shore, and the Taehwa River could reliably supply the enormous volumes of industrial water that large-scale plants require. Those two conditions turned Ulsan into the stage on which a resource-poor nation reinvented itself as an exporter of energy and petrochemical products.

| From Korea Oil Corporation to SK Innovation

At the center of that transformation was the company that wrote the first chapter of Korea’s oil industry — Korea Oil Corporation (Yukong), the direct ancestor of today’s SK Innovation.

Launched in October 1962 as Korea’s first state-run refiner alongside the country’s First Five-Year Economic Development Plan, the company broke ground the following year on the nation’s first oil refinery, in the open fields of Gosa-dong, Ulsan. Korea had neither the technology nor the capital to do this alone, so the project moved forward through a joint venture with the U.S. energy company Gulf Oil.

In 1964, the No. 1 Crude Distillation Unit — capacity 35,000 barrels per day — was completed and began commercial operation. That modest plant on an empty field marked the beginning of energy self-sufficiency for Korea.

In 1980, Sunkyong (today’s SK Group) acquired the company, completing an integrated business chain running from crude oil all the way to textiles. Six decades later, that first refinery has grown into SK Innovation Ulsan Complex (Ulsan CLX), a global petrochemical hub processing roughly 840,000 barrels of crude per day.

| 600,000 Kilometers of Pipeline on a Site Larger Than Central Park

Approach the Yongyeon and Gosa-dong area of southern Ulsan and an industrial landscape opens up in front of you on a scale that is difficult to process. Ulsan CLX covers about 8.26 million square meters — roughly 2.4 times the size of New York’s Central Park, or the equivalent of some 1,100 football pitches. As a single integrated petrochemical complex, it is the largest of its kind in the world.

Inside, SK’s core energy and chemical affiliates — SK Energy, SK Geo Centric and SK Enmove — operate side by side as a single interconnected ecosystem. Crude oil arriving at the terminal travels through subsea pipelines to be refined at a rate of about 840,000 barrels a day, and the resulting streams are converted into roughly 7.7 million tons of petrochemical products and high-performance lubricants each year.

The most striking number, though, is the piping. The total length of pipeline running through Ulsan CLX is approximately 600,000 kilometers — longer than the distance from the Earth to the Moon (about 380,000 km), and enough to circle the planet fifteen times. Through those silver capillaries, the fuels and materials that keep Korea’s economy running flow without pause, 24 hours a day.

| An Industrial Frontline That Grew a Forest — and a Rose Garden

Ulsan is a city where you can hear people working.

At lunchtime, engineers in hard hats and coveralls fill the restaurants around the industrial complex, cooling off and eating together before heading back in. It is a very particular kind of energy, and it says a lot about how this city sees itself.

But life in the shadow of a non-stop industrial zone came at a cost. For decades, Ulsan residents lived with air pollution and a serious shortage of green space — the familiar trade-off of rapid industrialization.

In 1995, Chey Jong-hyon, the late chairman of SK Group, made a promise: “SK grew thanks to the support of the people of Ulsan, and we want to return the fruits of that growth to them.” He committed the company to building a large public park.

Construction continued even through the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, when Korean companies were cutting everything they could. Over ten years, SK invested more than 100 billion Korean won to complete Ulsan Grand Park — 3.64 million square meters, slightly larger than Central Park — and in 2006 donated the entire park to the city of Ulsan free of charge.

The partnership did not end there. Every May, the park’s rose garden hosts the Ulsan Grand Park Rose Festival, co-organized by SK and the city. With more than three million roses in bloom, it has become one of Ulsan’s signature cultural events, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors from across the country.

A forest, a rose garden and a lake in the middle of what was once a gray industrial city: today they are where Ulsan’s residents go to rest. It is also one of Korea’s most frequently cited examples of a company and a community growing together.

| Ulsan’s Next Chapter: Clean Energy and AI

Just as that green space changed daily life in Ulsan, the city is now changing something deeper — the makeup of its industry itself. After six decades of supplying the energy that powered Korea’s growth, Ulsan is attempting a far more ambitious pivot.

Ulsan CLX sits at the center of it, and the transformation has two axes: clean energy and AI.

Moving beyond conventional petroleum fuels, Ulsan CLX has begun Korea’s first commercial production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), produced from feedstocks such as used cooking oil and capable of dramatically reducing lifecycle carbon emissions in aviation. The complex is also building out a clean hydrogen ecosystem spanning production, storage and distribution.

Inside the plant, digital transformation is reshaping day-to-day operations. Rather than buying an off-the-shelf solution, SK Innovation developed Smart Plant 2.0 in-house, encoding sixty years of accumulated field know-how. More than 40 Smart Plant 2.0 projects — applying AI and digital technology across process operations, equipment management and SHE (Safety, Health, Environment) — are now deployed on site. AI systems control processes while robot dogs and drones patrol for safety hazards. Behind them is a workforce of roughly 90 Citizen Data Scientists and 10 AI/DT specialists solving problems directly on the shop floor.

The ambition extends beyond the fence line. The Ulsan Forum, first proposed by SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won in 2022 and co-hosted by SK and the Ulsan Chamber of Commerce and Industry with support from the Ulsan Metropolitan Government, brings local small and mid-sized manufacturers into the conversation about AI Transformation (AX) in manufacturing — spreading the benefits of technological change across the whole city.

Now in its fifth edition, the 2026 Ulsan Forum runs under the slogan “Leading AX, Smart Life Ulsan,” organized around two themes: the workplace and the living space. It takes place on Friday, September 11 at the Ulsan Exhibition & Convention Center (UECO), held jointly with the Ulsan World Advanced Industry Expo (WAVE) to give visitors a hands-on look at manufacturing AX and smart city strategy.

From a quiet harbor where whales once swam, to the industrial heart that drove a nation’s economic rise. Now, with AI as its new engine, Ulsan is preparing for one more leap — this time as a global hub for advanced industry.

ATR considers manufacturing in India as regional air travel drives need for 200-300 more aircraft

ATR CEO Nathalie Tarnaud Laude said even a modest increase in air travel between India's smaller cities could create demand for 200-300 additional regional aircraft, potentially supporting local manufacturing.

Advertisement

By Abhimanyu Sharma

Regional aircraft manufacturer ATR is considering India as a potential manufacturing location as it expects growing demand for air travel between smaller cities to create the need for additional production capacity.

ATR CEO Nathalie Tarnaud Laude said the company could require additional manufacturing capacity for components to support demand for 200-300 aircraft in India, making the country a potential location for such production.

Speaking to CNBC-TV18's Abhimanyu Sharma on the sidelines of FLY91's aircraft-order signing ceremony in New Delhi, Laude described India as a “promising” market and pointed to the government's UDAN scheme, which seeks to improve air connectivity to underserved parts of the country.

Indian regional carrier FLY91 on Thursday placed an order for 40 ATR 72-600 aircraft, in a deal valued at around $1 billion. The companies said it was the largest ATR order placed globally by a regional airline.

ATR sees room for sharp growth in regional flying

Laude cited a study conducted last year on intercity travel between India's Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, which found that only around 3% of such trips were made by air, compared with 7-9% in other countries.

Even a 0.7 percentage point increase in the share of Indians travelling by air could translate into an additional 45 million air passengers, she said.

Meeting that demand could require another 200-300 ATR aircraft, significantly more than the roughly 70 ATR planes currently operating in India, according to Laude.

The expected increase in aircraft requirements is also prompting ATR to consider whether part of the additional manufacturing capacity needed to meet that demand could be located in India.

ATR is a joint venture between Airbus and Leonardo and manufactures the ATR 42 and ATR 72 turboprop aircraft, which cater to the sub-90-seat regional aircraft market.

According to the company, ATR aircraft are operated by around 200 airlines across more than 100 countries, with operators opening an average of 120 new routes annually.

ATR and FLY91 said in a joint statement that smaller regional aircraft can help connect remote areas and improve access to services such as healthcare and education.

The companies also said ATR aircraft emit 45% less carbon dioxide than similar-sized regional jets. In January 2022, an ATR aircraft operated what the company described as the first commercial flight using 100% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in both engines.

text:
[SINGAPORE] A green jet fuel levy for air cargo will be deferred for a year and start from Oct 1, 2027, for flights leaving Singapore from Jan 1, 2028.

In a statement on Sept 3, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) said the air cargo levy is being pushed back because of the diverse nature of air cargo and the number of businesses and agencies involved, compared with passenger flights.

These include airlines, freight forwarders and shippers, with different commercial arrangements in place.

CAAS said: “Taking into account industry feedback, the one-year deferment will allow more time for CAAS to work with the industry to develop and implement a robust, sustainable aviation fuel levy collection mechanism for cargo shipments on departing flights.”

CAAS earlier said travellers booking flights out of Singapore will be required to pay a jet fuel green levy from Jan 1, 2027, if they buy tickets from Oct 1.

The levy will go towards the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel.

Passengers in economy or premium economy class will pay between S$1 and S$10.40, depending on their destination. Those who fly business or first class will pay between S$4 and S$41.60.

This is based on industry norms for calculating the carbon emissions of passengers in different cabin classes.

Industry players welcomed the move to defer the air cargo green fuel levy.

Gabriel Lam, chairman of SAAA@Singapore – formerly the Singapore Aircargo Agents Association – said trying to adopt a “one size fits all” approach for the industry when collecting levies could create inconsistencies.

By extending the runway for implementation, industry players can navigate the transition in a “more measured and sustainable manner”, he added.

The extra lead time, he said, can help companies to plan ahead and communicate with their customers and partners before the fee takes effect.

The green jet fuel levy was supposed to take effect for passengers flying out of Singapore in October with tickets bought from April 1.

However, it was pushed back to Jan 1, 2027, in response to the global energy crisis brought on by the Middle East war, which saw the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s global oil and energy supply flows.

As longer flights consume more fuel, travellers who fly to farther destinations will pay a higher levy.

The fee will be reflected as a distinct item in the fare breakdown.

To apply the levy, destinations worldwide have been grouped into four geographical bands, with the levy amount increasing with each successive band, based on the distance travelled.

The bands are South-east Asia (Band 1); North-east Asia, South Asia, Australia and Papua New Guinea (Band 2); Africa, Central and West Asia, Europe, the Middle East, the Pacific Islands and New Zealand (Band 3); and the Americas (Band 4).

Airfreight stakeholders have responded positively to the decision of Singapore’s government to delay the implementation of a new green levy for cargo as the industry wrestles with the practicalities of meeting its environmental pledges.

In a statement issued this morning (3 September) the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore said it will “defer the implementation of the levy for air cargo shipments by one year to apply to services sold from 1 October 2027 for flights departing Singapore from 1 January 2028”.

Director-general of CAAS, Han Kok Juan, added: “CAAS has worked closely with airlines and other global industry partners to set up a robust regime for levy collection, procurement and environmental attributes management.

“In doing so, CAAS seeks to lay the foundation for Singapore to serve as a trusted hub for SAF-related economic activities in the region,” Mr Han added, with the aviation authority noting that it was still rolling out its planned levy for passenger services.

Explaining its reasoning, CAAS noted that compared with passenger operations, cargo services involve a broader range of stakeholders – notably carriers, express operators, forwarders, and shippers – all operating under “varying commercial arrangements”.

Following industry engagement, it agreed rolling out the levy from the start of next month for flights departing 1 January 2027 would prove problematic and as such said that it had agreed “to work with industry to develop and implement a robust SAF Levy collection mechanism”.

Unsurprisingly, industry has responded positively, stakeholders telling The Loadstar a delay was necessary, with chair of Singaporean air cargo agents association SAAA@Singapore, Gabriel Lam noting a “one size fits all” approach for passenger and cargo did not make sense.

Mr Lam told local outlets that moving ahead without adapting the system for collecting levies for the more diffuse make-up of the airfreight sector would lead to inconsistencies leading to unsustainable cost price spikes.

He added that the additional lead time would allow companies to not only better plan for the levy’s implementation but to make clear to their customers what the additional costs would be and when they would be due, offering a “more measured and sustainable” transition.

A spokesperson for Kuehne+Nagel responded to a request for comment from The Loadstar by saying that the company “supports mandates that help drive greater adoption of SAF and provide producers with the confidence to invest in additional production capacity”.

While not responding directly to questions about the decision of the Singaporean regulator to delay its own levy’s introduction, the spokesperson noted that these mandates were being introduced “at different speeds and through different mechanisms”.

Another source working in the field told The Loadstar that they would not comment publicly – “and I am not surprised others haven’t” – because they said the issue of SAF and levies “is, to some extent, a contentious one, but they should be supported”.

text:
Global ocean-based shipping company Norden announced the completion of a new pilot transaction with Microsoft, marking the first delivery of verified emissions reduction by a maritime carrier through the RSB Book & Claim Registry.

Launched in 2022 by the Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB) with an initial focus on aviation, the RSB Book & Claim system was created to help manage and monitor a book and claim system to expand the ability of companies to access sustainable fuels for hard to abate sectors. Book & Claim allows companies to purchase verified emissions reductions linked to sustainable fuels, regardless of where those fuels are consumed.

The new transaction follows the launch of a pilot by Microsoft and Norden last year to help the tech giant reduce its maritime supply chain emissions through Norden’s biofuel voyage and Book and Claim solution, with the companies engaging with RSB to update its book and claim system to enable credible tracking of sustainable maritime fuel claims. The pilot targeted the reduction of Microsoft’s maritime Scope 3 emissions by nearly 10,000 tonnes of CO2e over a three year period.

Norden said that it aims to scale the solution with the goal of making verified emissions reductions a standard offering in ocean transport. The company added that the solution will enable its direct customers and clients in other industries which are dependent on marine transportation and seeking to decarbonize their supply chains to credibly invest in maritime decarbonization.

Norden said that in order to enable the transaction, the company became the first maritime operator to obtain RSB Book & Claim trader certification, a prerequisite for issuing and selling verified emissions reductions through the RSB’s Book & Claim registry. The certification was developed in close collaboration with RSB, which extended its existing aviation framework to cover maritime transport and carriers.

Anne Jensen, COO at Norden, said:

“For many companies, some of the most difficult emissions to address are those embedded deep within global supply chains, where they often have little visibility or direct influence over how goods are transported. This transaction demonstrates how Book & Claim can help bridge that gap. By enabling companies to invest in verified emissions reductions from maritime transport, regardless of where the fuel is used or where they sit in the value chain, we can help accelerate decarbonisation across industries.”

Microsoft is the first company globally to use Book & Claim for shipping emissions through the RSB registry, forming part of its broader efforts to address value chain emissions, the companies said.

Bella Horstmann, Senior Manager, Market Development, Microsoft, said:

“Decarbonising supply chains requires solutions that are both credible and scalable. This collaboration with NORDEN and RSB shows how Book & Claim can help accelerate progress in sectors where change is otherwise complex and demonstrates that companies don’t need to wait to start reducing their shipping emissions in a verified and meaningful way.”

text:
New analysis finds that a third runway at Heathrow would blow a hole in the UK’s ability to meet legally binding climate targets.

The case for aviation expansion hinges on sustainable aviation fuels and greenhouse gas removals but there is currently no evidence that these technologies can support the scale of expansion envisaged by the government.

The climate scientists behind the report recommend the government rejects plans for a third runway.

There is no credible scenario in which expansion at Heathrow can go ahead without blowing a hole in the UK’s legally binding climate targets, new modelling published by the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research at The University of Manchester reveals today.

The report, commissioned by the environmental justice organisation Friends of the Earth, provides the first detailed analysis of whether Heathrow expansion is compatible with the UK’s legal carbon budgets.

Recent approvals of airport expansion at Gatwick, Stansted Luton and many other locations mean that UK aviation is already projected to exceed its share of the Seventh Carbon Budget (2038-42) by between 21 and 50%, depending on how much sustainable aviation fuel materialises. That is before any Heathrow expansion takes place.

The analysis concludes that the two technologies relied upon to enable passenger growth or airport expansion to fit within carbon budgets – Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) and Greenhouse Gas Removals (GGR) – are not even close to being on track for sufficiently capacity within the required timeframe.

The report concludes that Heathrow expansion cannot credibly meet the UK’s climate targets thanks to three key findings:

Aviation emissions: The UK’s aviation sector will already exceed its share of the Seventh Carbon Budget by around 40%, even before Heathrow expansion is considered. The research highlights how even the government’s own modelling reaches a similar conclusion.

Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF): Based on existing evidence SAF would be unable to close the emissions gap. Even optimistic deployment of this technology would leave aviation above its carbon budget share. Previous studies have shown that current SAF production methods face major structural constraints or compete with agriculture for land and water, just as farmers have experienced what could be the worst harvest on record and are already warning about the impact of the climate crisis on food production.

Greenhouse Gas Removals (GGRs): GGR describes methods that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stores it long-term, such as bioenergy with carbon capture and storage. The report highlights how global GGR deployment is significantly off track and that no engineered removal plants are operating yet in the UK. Despite this, aviation emissions modelling heavily relies upon future potential GGR to offset additional emissions. Even before any airport expansion is taken into account aviation is the biggest projected user of GGR capacity. On top of this, these scenarios all depend on SAF pulling its weight; if SAF fails to deliver, even more GGR will have to be deployed. The report concludes that the building capacity for more aviation demand before large scale GGR facilities are operational is inconsistent with taking climate targets seriously.

Non-CO₂ impacts are not accounted for: Aviation's full warming effects are not captured within carbon budgets. Non-CO₂e impacts including from nitrogen oxides and contrails, account for around two-thirds of aviation's climate warming and should be incorporated into future climate targets.

What do the researchers say?

The lead researchers, Dr Lois Pennington, Professor Alice Larkin and Dr Chris Jones recommend decisionmakers reject any proposed expansion at Heathrow Airport.

Dr Lois Pennington, Research Fellow at the Tyndall Centre said:

“Every aviation scenario the UK Government has published overshoots the carbon budget Parliament has legislated, before a third runway at Heathrow is even taken into account.

“Our analysis shows that aviation cannot continue to grow if the sector is to make a proportionate contribution to meeting the UK’s carbon budgets. Sustainable aviation fuels and carbon removals can contribute to limiting aviation emissions, but there is currently no evidence that these technologies can support the scale of aviation expansion envisaged by the government.

“Further aviation expansion carries a significant risk of exacerbating climate impacts by relying on the growth of technologies that are unlikely to materialise in the timescale needed.

“The UK is experiencing another exceptionally hot summer, while record-breaking severe wildfires have burnt across Western Europe. The Government must reassess the case for expansion. Climate policy must be grounded in what we can demonstrate and evidence, rather than what we hope may become possible.”

Mike Childs, head of policy, science and research at Friends of the Earth, said:

"After this summer of record-breaking heat and nearly 3,000 excess deaths, this third runway is the equivalent of pouring petrol on a raging wildfire.

"The evidence is clear: there is no route where expansion at Heathrow can be in line with our legally binding climate targets. Suggesting that sustainable aviation fuel and greenhouse gas removals can enable airport expansion is simply trying to pull the wool over people’s eyes.

"The government has a choice: commit to taking action on the climate seriously, reject Heathrow expansion and constrain excessive flying, or abandon the UK's climate targets and future generations by giving the third runway the go ahead.

"With a weak economic case to support expansion set against a huge impact on the climate and communities, this is the opportunity for the new Prime Minister to truly set a precedent by turning his back to corporate lobbying and say no to a third runway at Heathrow."

The public consultation on the government's Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement (HENPS) closed earlier this week on Tuesday 1 September, the same day that members of parliament returned from recess to scrutinise the proposal.

Friends of the Earth and the Tyndall Centre are calling on the UK Government to reject Heathrow expansion and ensure future aviation policy remains consistent with legally binding carbon budgets under the Climate Change Act.
