text:
SAF production capacity expected to reach approximately 200 million gallon annual run rate by year-end 2028, with total renewable product sales expanded 40% to 17,000 barrels per day

Remaining project capital for this expansion reduced to $137 million from the $1.2 billion contemplated in the original Phase 2 plan, driven by the repurposing of proven equipment from the adjacent Calumet Montana Refining asphalt facility through a series of quick-payback steps

No third-party equity requirement provides simple capital structure and eliminates dilution, positioning MRL for future strategic opportunities; expansion is expected to be funded with Montana Renewables earnings alongside a final $34 million draw under a DOE loan

Calumet Montana Refining will continue to produce retail asphalt and provide shared site cost efficiencies across both businesses, preserving all Great Falls jobs

INDIANAPOLIS, Sept. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Calumet, Inc. (NASDAQ: CLMT) ("Calumet," "we," "our" or "us") announced today a new flight plan for its MaxSAF® expansion at Montana Renewables, LLC ("Montana Renewables" or "MRL"), an unrestricted subsidiary of Calumet. By repurposing proven, installed refining equipment from the adjacent Calumet Montana Refining ("CMR") facility, Montana Renewables expects to reach approximately 200 million gallons of annual Sustainable Aviation Fuel ("SAF") production and 17,000 barrels per day of total product sales by year-end 2028. The total remaining project capital spend for this expansion is $137 million, compared to the $1.2 billion megaproject contemplated in the original loan issued by the U.S. Department of Energy ("DOE") through its Office of Energy Dominance Financing ("EDF").

Reflecting the dramatically lower capital requirement, Montana Renewables and EDF have amended the Loan Guarantee Agreement ("LGA") originally executed in January 2025. Phase 2 DOE funding is reduced from up to $658 million to a single, final draw of $34 million, with the balance of the expansion self-funded from MRL earnings. The original agreement required the project's full equity to be committed before Phase 2 construction. The amended structure requires no third-party equity, thereby eliminating dilution and preserving a simple capital structure for future strategic opportunities while accelerating the benefits of increased throughput, SAF, improved yields, and reduced unit costs.

>> In Other News: Live Oak Starts Competitive FEED for Nebraska e-Methane

The centerpiece of the revised plan is the redeployment of selected CMR assets — a hydrotreater, hydrogen plant, and naphtha splitter — to Montana Renewables under a long-term lease. The tied-in hydrotreater creates a proprietary dual reactor system that runs in a "polishing" service rather than the industry-standard "cracking" service, delivering competitively advantaged SAF yields while lowering by-product production and reducing yield loss. Several additional modular components, including a third renewable fuels reactor currently offsite, provide the ability to expand capacity beyond 200 million gallons over time.

Rather than a single large construction project, the new expansion is structured as six small, controllable, quick-payback projects, each designed to increase returns and reduce construction risk. Following constraint removal completed at the Spring 2026 turnaround, Montana Renewables is currently producing at a run-rate of 60 million gallons of SAF per year; expects to exceed an 80 million gallon run-rate by year-end 2026; surpass 120 million gallons by Spring 2027; and reach approximately 200 million gallons by year-end 2028. The program also captures approximately 20 million gallons per year of renewable propane and butane — previously burned as fuel gas — as saleable product, improves renewable naphtha yields, and reduces unit operating costs through scale and lower water usage.

The reconfiguration represents the next evolution of more than a decade of modernization at the Great Falls site under Calumet's ownership. The turnaround to complete the tie-in is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026 — timing that allows CMR to capture approximately $50 million of EBITDA at currently elevated global refining margins before the transition. CMR will remain in service, continuing to produce high-quality retail asphalt, retaining all employees, and providing shared cost efficiencies across the full site.

"Our amended agreement with the DOE facilitates innovative technology and domestic energy security at a fraction of the original cost," said Todd Borgmann, CEO of Calumet. "EDF's willingness to right-size the LGA reflects its ongoing support for Montana's largest agricultural investment. We look forward to our continued collaboration with the DOE on the success of this project."

"We've worked hard to unleash the ingenuity of our engineering and operational teams, and they developed a project that captures approximately 70% of the originally expected benefit while spending only 15% of the originally expected Phase 2 capital," Borgmann continued. "The DOE has kept our nation's energy independence goals at the forefront while demonstrating tremendous flexibility in thoughtfully working with us to adjust the loan. MRL was honored to be the first project to receive the support of the current Administration, and we thank the entire DOE team for its continued commitment to this key component of America's energy infrastructure. With the DOE's support, Montana Renewables continues to strengthen its position as one of the world's largest SAF producers while supporting regional agriculture, the Montana business community, our employees, and our shareholders."

The expansion increases MRL's total feedstock consumption to approximately 2 billion pounds of ranch- and farm-originated feedstocks, converted into American-made renewable jet fuel, diesel, and gasoline annually, while continuing to grow Montana's wage and tax base with highly skilled technical employment in a rural community.

Amended Loan Guarantee Structure

The DOE loan remains structured in two tranches. The first tranche of $782 million was funded in February 2025 and used to recapitalize MRL, including an additional $150 million equity investment by Calumet with cash on hand. Under the amended agreement, the remaining loan availability is reduced to a single, final draw of $34 million — down significantly from the previous additional draw of up to $658 million, which MRL expects to receive shortly, subject to the satisfaction of certain commercial, technical, and legal conditions precedent.

During construction, retained earnings from MRL are expected to supplement DOE funds to maintain debt at less than 55% of eligible spending. The loan retains its 15-year tenor and an annual interest rate of the U.S. Treasury rate plus 3/8%, with servicing of principal and interest deferred until MaxSAF® is commissioned. The March 2029 first servicing date and December 2039 maturity remain unchanged. The amended LGA will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission ("SEC"), and investors should refer to the filed agreement for complete terms.

About Montana Renewables

Montana Renewables (MRL) is a leading renewable fuel company located in Great Falls, Montana. We produce Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), Renewable Diesel, Renewable Hydrogen, and Renewable Naphtha. As one of only three SAF producers running at commercial scale in North America, we meet the increasing demand for sustainable jet fuels. As a Great Falls business leader, MRL offers high-paying jobs and career opportunities while supporting the local economy and contributing to the community's overall well-being. Pacific Northwest farm and ranch operations ultimately provide MRL with sustainable, renewable, low-carbon feedstocks and agricultural byproducts including tallow, distillers corn oil, canola oil, used cooking oil and camelina oil. These are converted to renewable transportation fuels which have lower emissions compared to conventional fossil fuels. MRL is an unrestricted subsidiary of Calumet, Inc.

About Calumet

Calumet, Inc. (NASDAQ: CLMT) manufactures, formulates, and markets a diversified slate of specialty branded products and renewable fuels to customers across a broad range of consumer-facing and industrial markets. Calumet is headquartered in Indianapolis, Indiana and operates twelve facilities throughout North America.

title: SAF growth creates opportunities for agriculture, aviation and economic development
description:
The future of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) will depend on strong partnerships among farmers, fuel producers, the aviation industry and government leaders, according to panelists participating in a discussion during the 2026 Global Aerospace Summit in the St. Louis region.
She discussed how the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII) was established in Illinois two years ago following a state-led SAF summit convened at the governor's request.
That event brought together stakeholders from across the aviation fuel ecosystem and highlighted the need for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)-specific testing standards, technical expertise and workforce training.
The panel also highlighted the important role Midwest agriculture can play in supporting SAF and other renewable fuel feedstock production.
The conversation reinforced that SAF development is not solely an aviation initiative, but one that relies on coordination among agriculture, energy, transportation and economic development stakeholders.
text:
The future of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) will depend on strong partnerships among farmers, fuel producers, the aviation industry and government leaders, according to panelists participating in a discussion during the 2026 Global Aerospace Summit in the St. Louis region. During a session titled “The Future of Flight Runs on SAF,” attendees heard how Illinois, Missouri and the broader Midwest corn belt are positioned to play a leading role in expanding domestic SAF production while creating new opportunities for agricultural producers and strengthening the aviation industry.

Moderated by Darren James, director of MidAmerica St. Louis Airport, the panel featured Jim Hedges, CEO of CoverCress, an ag-tech company developing a winter oilseed crop grown between corn and soybean seasons, and Cindy Tomei, president of the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII). The discussion focused on the current state of the SAF industry, the need for investment in production and infrastructure, and the critical role agriculture will play in meeting growing demand for lower-carbon aviation fuels.

“Illinois has emerged as a leader in the SAF space, with industry, government and research organizations collaborating to attract projects and advance the sector,” Tomei said.

She discussed how the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII) was established in Illinois two years ago following a state-led SAF summit convened at the governor's request. That event brought together stakeholders from across the aviation fuel ecosystem and highlighted the need for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)-specific testing standards, technical expertise and workforce training. She said, today, the Institute, which is headquartered in Sugar Grove, Illinois, serves as a hub for SAF education, testing and industry collaboration. It provides hands-on laboratory training in fuel testing, helps organizations understand SAF properties and blending considerations, and connects stakeholders across the global SAF supply chain.

Discussing recent progress in the SAF industry, Tomei said it has been accelerated by greater clarity around the federal 45Z tax credit and improvements in calculating carbon intensity scores, which help determine incentive eligibility.

At the same time, growing global demand, including sustainable aviation fuel mandates across the European Union and continuing challenges moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz, has increased awareness of SAF and heightened the urgency to scale production and deployment. As demand for sustainable aviation fuel continues to accelerate, Tomei said it’s increasingly important to build the infrastructure needed to move fuel from production facilities to airports. She noted that O'Hare is in one of the top 10 airports for SAF procurement worldwide.

“Speed is really of the essence, whether it is getting SAF scaled up regardless of what the feedstock is, but also having the right infrastructure to get it transported, stored and blended with jet fuel, so that it can actually be used,” Tomei said.

The panel also highlighted the important role Midwest agriculture can play in supporting SAF and other renewable fuel feedstock production. Hedges, whose company continued to hit significant milestones over the past year, noted that meeting future demand will require additional feedstocks and innovative crops that can complement existing farming operations while providing new revenue opportunities from existing acreage for producers.

“I see a huge role for Midwest agriculture,” Hedges said. “We’re crushing so many soybean acres already, but there’s no new soybean acres coming in. As all types of renewable fuels use continue to grow, we need to have supply to fulfill the demand. You have to have these new types of crops... canola, camelina, as well as CoverCress. These are crops that are planted when ground is fallow so they are truly additive to the supply of feedstock. We want everybody to be successful, because I think our biggest challenge is not meeting the demand.”

The discussion underscored how emerging feedstocks and technologies can position farmers as increasingly important participants in the future aviation fuel supply chain. Hedges explained the importance of raising awareness about the opportunity to easily grow an additional crop between corn and soybean seasons, creating a new revenue stream for farmers while improving soil health. Panelists noted that continued innovation, adoption of new crops and closer coordination throughout the production process will be essential to scaling the SAF and other renewable fuels industry.

Hedges stressed that collaboration across the fuel production ecosystem must begin early in the development process, particularly because federal Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) pathway approvals can take years. Hedges noted that CoverCress Inc just hit a major milestone with obtaining the first RFS pathway approval for CoverCress Oil, which took 2.5 years from the time the pathway was submitted.

“The earlier coordination with refiners can begin with these new crops, the better,” Hedges said. “Establish a relationship with one or more refiners. Get your pathways going as you’re doing your product development. And that way, when the product is commercially viable, it’s probably going to be around the time that you get these RFS pathway approvals.”

Panelists also discussed the rigorous testing and quality controls required for aviation fuels, the need for supportive public policies and the importance of ensuring adequate production capacity. The conversation reinforced that SAF development is not solely an aviation initiative, but one that relies on coordination among agriculture, energy, transportation and economic development stakeholders.

Looking ahead, Tomei encouraged greater collaboration among the many organizations already advancing SAF initiatives throughout Illinois. “Illinois really is a leader,” Tomei said. “There are so many good things happening in different pockets on an individual basis with SAF that, if we brought it together, we’d be an even stronger powerhouse.”

For farmers and agricultural organizations, the growth of SAF represents an opportunity to help supply a developing domestic fuel market through both established commodities and new crops, supporting farm revenue, sustainability goals and domestic energy security. “Right now, we're all kind of in that early ramp up stage, but we are planning to have hundreds of thousands of acres of these new innovative crops by the early 2030s,” Hedges said.

The event was presented by the Leadership Council Southwestern Illinois, Madison County and St. Clair County, Illinois, and Bi-State Development’s St. Louis Regional Freightway. title: A Machine That Eats CO2 and Outputs 475,000 Gallons of Water! - Yahoo Tech
description:
Direct air capture has spent years collecting hype and pilot projects; Project Brighton, Avnos' new facility in Bridgewater, New Jersey, is meant to collect something more useful — operational data.
Two Outputs, One Machine This New Jersey facility doesn't just pull carbon from the air — it produces clean water as a byproduct, without requiring external heat.
Standard direct air capture pulls carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stops there.
Avnos' Hybrid Direct Air Capture system — HDAC — claims to do that while simultaneously producing water, and without requiring external heat to run.
Brighton says it can capture up to 450 tons of CO2 annually alongside those 475,000 gallons of water.
text:
475,000 gallons of clean water. That's supposedly what falls out the other side of a machine designed to eat CO2. Direct air capture has spent years collecting hype and pilot projects; Project Brighton, Avnos' new facility in Bridgewater, New Jersey, is meant to collect something more useful — operational data. The U.S. Office of Naval Research thought that was worth funding. That's not nothing.

Two Outputs, One Machine

This New Jersey facility doesn't just pull carbon from the air — it produces clean water as a byproduct, without requiring external heat.

Standard direct air capture pulls carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stops there. Avnos' Hybrid Direct Air Capture system — HDAC — claims to do that while simultaneously producing water, and without requiring external heat to run. Brighton says it can capture up to 450 tons of CO2 annually alongside those 475,000 gallons of water. Whether those numbers hold under sustained real-world conditions is exactly what the Bridgewater site exists to find out.

"Brighton demonstrates our ability to deliver infrastructure at increasing scale," said Will Kain, citing the facility's role generating "real-world performance data" for future commercial deployments.

Brighton isn't saving the planet. It's running the experiment that determines whether saving the planet is actually on the table.

Pentagon Money and Jet Fuel: The Bigger Picture

Defense funding for carbon removal is less surprising than it sounds — the Navy has a documented sustainable aviation fuel shortage, and captured CO2 is a direct feedstock candidate.

The U.S. Office of Naval Research backed Brighton for a reason. Jet fuel made from captured atmospheric carbon isn't science fiction; it's an active development pathway, and the Navy has strong institutional incentive to see it work. Brighton's output is reportedly intended to feed exactly that — turning atmospheric carbon into sustainable aviation fuel inputs. It's still an intended application, not a confirmed pipeline, so treat the SAF angle as directional rather than delivered.

Chris Edwards described the project as evidence of technology companies "building real infrastructure at scale." Avnos is backing that claim with more than one site. Project Cedar, a second HDAC deployment with up to $17 million in project financing, is designed to test whether Avnos can build faster and repeat the process more cheaply. Brighton writes the playbook; Cedar stress-tests it.

text:
As the USDA’s regenerative agricultural feedstock framework moves toward implementation under the 45Z clean fuel production credit, attention is growing towards reallocating reduced-carbon intensity (CI) feedstock between separately located, but commonly owned elevators.

While this approach may make sense on a corporate ledger, it runs into a fundamental question of mass balance. Can the reduced-CI attribute move where the physical grain does not?

Our conclusion at Christianson is no. USDA’s definition of mass balance, its alignment with ISO 22095:2020, our discussions with USDA staff and final rule authors, and USDA’s August 18 webinar all support the same conclusion: mass balance follows the physical flow of the feedstock.

That distinction is important as renewable fuel producers, elevators and other supply-chain entities prepare for implementation of the USDA framework and its anticipated incorporation into the 45ZCF-GREET model.

USDA established a mass-balance system for tracking reduced-CI material as it moves through the supply chain. The final rule requires applicable first points of aggregation and intermediary entities (i.e., elevators, traders, and processors) to account for incoming and outgoing reduced-CI crops so that the quantities balance over defined periods.

That is where the multiple-location entity question becomes important.

Consider an entity with two grain storage facilities. A farmer produces qualifying reduced-CI corn and delivers it to Location A. Location B is closer to a renewable fuel producer, but the grain at Location B is conventional.

Because both facilities are owned by the same entity, some companies may want to argue the two locations should be treated as one inventory pool and allow 10,000 bushels of reduced-CI corn received at Location A, to be sold from Location B with no physical movement of the grain.

While this approach may be considered appropriate in some circumstances, ISO 22095-2 leaves the location-specific detail up to the system that is applying its chain of custody protocol, the USDA. Under the USDA final rule, the entity mass balancing without physical movement of grain is not a permissible mass-balance approach.

The definition in the USDA final rule for a mass balance system requires that “…materials or products with specified characteristics are mixed with materials or products without some or all of these characteristics…”. Therefore, the reduced-CI grain must physically move and be mixed with conventional grain in order to mass balance at any given entity in the supply chain. Common ownership alone does not allow an entity to transfer the reduced-CI attribute from one physical location to another without also moving physical product.

Grains are not required to be mixed

Another heavily referenced area in this discussion is in the Applicability section of the regulation, which notes, “Reduced-CI crops and conventional crops can be physically mixed,” which implies that they are not required to be physically mixed.

Christianson agrees with this statement, however it applies to the program as a whole, not specifically to a mass balance system. Traders who purchase grain, but do not take physical possession of the grain, are still an entity in the supply chain and subject to audit.

These traders will not implement a mass balance system, because they never take physical possession of the grain and mix it with conventional grain or other reduced-CI grain. Any entity in the supply chain that does not mix physical products together is required to pass through the feedstock certificates from its supplier to its customer.

USDA has addressed the issue

text:
XCF Global Inc., a scaling U.S.-based producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), on Sept. 1 announced another milestone in the company's transition from development-stage operations to active, revenue-generating commercial production.

The company's flagship New Rise Renewables Reno facility has produced 886,400 gallons of renewable diesel to date. This production milestone supports two potential revenue streams: direct physical fuel sales and renewable identification numbers (RINs) generated under the U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard. XCF has monetized 550,000 D4 RINs at $2.27 per RIN, representing approximately $1.25 million in value, with settlement expected to conclude on Sept. 2, 2026.

Production at New Rise Reno began in early July 2026, marking the facility's transition from commissioning activities to active fuel production. Customer shipments began in early August, and the facility is currently fulfilling orders at approximately 55,000 gallons per day. At nameplate capacity, New Rise Reno is designed to produce approximately 90,000 gallons per day, representing up to 38 million gallons per year of permitted production capacity, subject to production volumes, logistics, customer demand, market conditions and other factors.

The renewable diesel produced to date has also generated more than 1.5 million D4 RINs under the U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard, creating a potential value stream in addition to physical fuel sales. The $2.27 per RIN transaction price reflects the actual monetization transaction rather than an estimated market value and remains subject to final settlement, timing of transfer, transaction costs, regulatory requirements and other adjustments.

XCF expects New Rise Reno to begin producing synthetic blending component for use in sustainable aviation fuel in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to operations, market conditions, regulatory requirements, customer demand and other factors.

text:
Expander Energy will use Axens FT Liquid Upgrading technology to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel made from cellulosic raw materials in Canada.

The Canadian company selected Axens as the supplier of Fischer-Tropsch (FT) fluid enhancement technology for its biofuel projects second generation. The solution will be integrated with Expander Energy’s patented EBTL® and BETL® processes to obtain liquid fuels compatible with the existing energy infrastructure.

The technology will initially be implemented in two commercial projects, one is the Wheatland Bio-Synfuels Facility, near Calgary, Alberta, and the second is the Mackenzie Biomass Derived E-Fuels Facility, located in northern British Columbia.

In addition, Expander Energy selected Axens as a strategic supplier for a broader portfolio of projects aimed at producing SAF and renewable diesel, including fuels geared towards Arctic applications.

FT technology to transform biomass into fuels

FT Liquid Upgrading technologyAxens will form part of the process developed by Expander Energy to convert cellulosic raw materials into second generation biofuels.

Its application will be linked to two technologies patented by the Canadian company, one of which is Enhanced Biomass to Liquids (EBTL®) and the other one is Biomass Electrolysis to Liquids (BETL®).

Through these processes, Expander aims to produce liquid fuels that can be integrated into existing distribution and consumption chains without requiring significant infrastructure changes. Key products include sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel.

The company is considering using forestry and agricultural waste as raw materials, this approach allows for the use of cellulosic resources to produce fuels with lower carbon intensity and to diversify the sources used in the manufacture of biofuels.

Axens, for its part, provides technologies related to the conversion of oil and biomass into fuels, as well as solutions for refining, natural gas treatment, carbon capture and the production of petrochemical intermediates.

Expander Energy moves forward with two projects in Canada

The first commercial application of the technology is planned for the Wheatland Bio-Synfuels Facility, located near Calgary, in Alberta.

The second project will be the Mackenzie Biomass Derived E-Fuels Facility, located in northern British Columbia. Both facilities are part of Expander Energy’s strategy to expand Canadian production of synthetic fuels derived from biomass.

Currently, both projects are progressing through their respective regulatory and financial processes, and the company aims to reach the final investment decision (FID) in December 2026. The FID will be a decisive step, as it will allow us to define the progress towards the commercial execution of the facilities and the development of the next stages of construction.

Axens will support a broader portfolio of SAF and renewable diesel

The collaboration between the two companies will not be limited to the projects in Alberta and British Columbia, Expander Energy also selected Axens as a strategic supplier of upgrade technology for other developments aimed at the production of sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel intended, among other uses, for the Arctic market.

In this way, FT Liquid Upgrading technology will have a broader role within Expander Energy’s portfolio, supporting the development of new routes to transform biomass into lower carbon-intensity liquid fuels.

text:
How integration gives Phillips 66 the reach to deliver

In this Today & Tomorrow feature, we take a closer look at the company’s integrated approach region by region, beginning with the West Coast, where energy demand is shaped by distance, geography, regulation, consumer expectations and some of the most dynamic fuel markets in the country.

Why it matters

Meeting evolving energy demand takes an integrated system that can adapt quickly to changing market needs while reliably supplying the fuels and products consumers depend on every day.

For investors, integration supports disciplined value creation.

For employees, it shows how their work connects to a larger enterprise.

For customers, it supports reliable supply and practical solutions.

For branded marketers and station operators, it helps connect trusted fuel brands with the supply, logistics and relationships behind them.

This approach maximizes efficiency, stability and opportunity in a volatile industry where every second counts.

Integration

Creating value from molecules to markets

The Phillips 66 Rodeo Renewable Energy Complex and Ferndale Refinery are at the center of the value chain, producing transportation fuels and products that make modern life possible.

Sourcing supply: The Phillips 66 Commercial team sources feedstocks, including crude and renewable feedstocks such as vegetable oil, used cooking oil and greases from domestic and global markets while identifying new market opportunities.

Moving products: Feedstocks and finished products are safely transported by an extensive Midstream network of pipelines and terminals in California, Oregon and Washington, as well as by rail, barge/vessel and truck.

In Los Angeles and Portland, our lubricants plants show how shared infrastructure and close coordination with Midstream create value across the system. Together, the sites use integrated marine, rail and tank farm capabilities to receive base oils and finished products such as motor oils, transmission fluids, turbine oil and hydraulic fluid — extending our value chain into the products that keep vehicles and industrial equipment running smoothly.

Connecting with consumers: The iconic 76® brand brings the system to life at the pump by connecting fuel supply to everyday consumer demand. Relationships with branded marketers, dealers and fuel station operators, along with our evolving Fuel Forward® loyalty platform and high-impact advertising and sponsorships with the Seattle Seahawks, San Francisco 49ersand Los Angeles Dodgers, builds familiarity, relevance and loyalty for 76.

Supply

Connecting resources to demand

While meeting today’s needs is essential, our business strategy also means we’re planning for future regional needs.

Supplying the West Coast: In Washington, the Phillips 66 Ferndale Refinery produces gasoline, diesel and California Reformulated Gasoline Blendstock for Oxygenate Blending. CARBOB is a California-regulated gasoline blend that helps supply the West Coast market and, more specifically, Northern California. The refinery is also enhancing its capabilities to support aviation fuel.

Rodeo’s marine dock, storage, transportation infrastructure and connections to Phillips 66’s integrated network form strategic links allowing renewable feedstocks to be sourced from around the world and efficiently transformed into renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel for consumers across the region.

Feedstocks and finished products move across the region through:

Marine terminals in Los Angeles, Rodeo and Portland.

Fuel product terminals in Torrance and Los Angeles, including the Torrance Tank Farm and terminals in Washington.

Associated pipelines in California.

Building future flexibility: The proposed Western Gateway Pipeline project is designed to improve supply flexibility, versatility and reliability by connecting Midcontinent and Gulf Coast refinery supply with growing markets in Arizona and California.

Evolution

Meeting today’s energy needs while building for the future

Advancing lower-carbon solutions: Rodeo represents both longevity and evolution as it celebrates its 130th birthday this year. After its transition from a traditional refinery in 2024, it’s now one of the largest renewable fuels facilities in the world, processing about 800 million gallons per year of renewable feedstocks to produce renewable diesel and SAF.

That leadership matters across the West Coast. Rodeo supplies SAF to aviation customers at major airports and renewable diesel to more than 600 76® branded stores.

Looking ahead: Phillips 66’s commitment to the region is reflected in a strong integrated system that keeps essential energy moving safely and reliably where and when it matters most. That integration will remain essential to reliable West Coast supply and evolving energy needs.

text:
Das US-Start-up Heart Aerospace hat am 12. August 2026 mit dem Erstflug seines batterieelektrischen Demonstrators X1 einen Etappensieg erzielt: Das Flugzeug mit über 11,3 Tonnen Startgewicht ist das bislang größte batteriebetriebene Flugzeug der Welt und flog 27 Minuten über dem US-Bundesstaat New York.

Mit Kaufabsichten für über 250 Maschinen im Wert von 9,4 Milliarden US-Dollar und einer geplanten Indienststellung ab 2031 zeigt Heart Aerospace, dass der Markt für alternative Kurzstrecken-Regionalflugzeuge trotz aller technischen Herausforderungen real ist.

X1 vs. ES-30: Versuchsflugzeug und Zielprodukt - 00:00:42

Die X1 ist baulich zwar in der Größenordnung der späteren ES-30 (Full Scale), fliegt aber zu 100 Prozent batterieelektrisch. Die geplante ES-30 wird dagegen einen Hybridantrieb aus Batterie und Kerosin erhalten. Rein elektrisch soll die ES-30 rund 200 km zurücklegen können, im Hybridbetrieb bis zu 800 km. Idealerweise soll dabei 100 Prozent Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) eingesetzt werden. Die ES-30 ist als 30-sitziges Regionalflugzeug konzipiert und soll ab 2031 in den Liniendienst gehen.

Strategiewechsel: Von der ES-19 zur ES-30 - 00:04:40

2021 bestellte United Airlines 100 Exemplare der rein elektrischen ES-19 (19 Sitze). 2022 verwarf Heart Aerospace diese Pläne vollständig. Der Grund: Die Kunden forderten ein größeres Flugzeug, und die heutige Batterietechnologie erlaube bei dieser Größe keine ausreichende Reichweite rein elektrisch. Der Hybridantrieb ermögliche zudem, gesetzlich vorgeschriebene Sicherheitsreserven über das konventionelle System abzudecken. Air Canada bestellte daraufhin 30 Exemplare der ES-30 und beteiligte sich zusammen mit Saab mit je 5 Millionen US-Dollar direkt am Unternehmen.

Marktumfeld, Wettbewerb und Ausblick - 00:07:18

Ein erstes Vorserienmodell (X2) mit Hybridantrieb entsteht aktuell in Los Angeles; die Flugerprobung der X2 soll 2028 beginnen. Kaufabsichten für über 250 ES-30 im Wert von 9,4 Milliarden US-Dollar liegen vor. Zum Wettbewerb: Eviation musste Anfang 2025 die Entwicklung ihres Projekts "Alice" stoppen. Airbus entwickelt mit Projekt „LEIA" eine hybrid-elektrische Architektur, die Demonstration ist geplant für 2027. GE Aerospace absolvierte erstmals einen hybrid-elektrisch unterstützten Flug in großer Höhe. ZeroAvia setzt auf Wasserstoffantrieb und erhielt kürzlich die Zulassung als Entwicklungsorganisation in Großbritannien.

text:
Burckhardt Compression has secured two orders to supply six process gas compressor packages and related services for the Boaventura Energy Complex, a major Petrobras energy project in Itaboraí, Rio de Janeiro. The orders are part of three parallel projects being executed at the complex by engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies. The compressor packages will support natural gas processing, as well as new refining and lubricant production facilities.

The project marks an important step in Burckhardt Compression’s plans to expand its business in South America. The Boaventura Energy Complex, formerly known as Comperj, is an important part of Petrobras’ plans to reduce the carbon intensity of its energy operations. Andreas Brautsch, President, Systems Division at Burckhardt Compression, said Brazil is one of South America’s most important energy hubs and a strategic market for the company. “Winning this order from Petrobras is a significant success for our team and a strong validation of our commitment to the region,” MR Brautsch said. text:
Washington: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has announced its decisions on 2025 Small Refinery Exemptions (SREs) and plans to reallocate renewable fuel obligations associated with exempted volumes, a move aimed at protecting demand for ethanol and biodiesel produced by US farmers and biofuel companies, according to press release.

US Representative Zach Nunn of Iowa welcomed the announcement, saying the reallocation would prevent biofuel demand lost through refinery exemptions from being permanently erased.

“Iowa’s farmers and biofuel producers built the most productive renewable fuel economy in the world,” Nunn said, adding that exempted biofuel volumes should be reallocated rather than removed from the market.

Under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), refiners are generally required to meet renewable fuel obligations through Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs). Small refinery exemptions allow eligible refineries to receive relief from these obligations. Critics have argued that exemptions can reduce demand for ethanol and biodiesel when the exempted volumes are not restored.

Nunn said he had pushed the EPA, along with other members of the Iowa delegation, to ensure that any volumes covered by the exemptions would be restored. He said the proposed reallocation would help protect demand for Iowa-grown corn-based ethanol and soybean-based biodiesel.

However, he stressed that the process is not complete until the EPA finalises the proposed rule and restores the affected renewable fuel volumes.

“If EPA grants refinery exemptions, those gallons need to be fully restored,” Nunn said, while also calling on Congress to advance permanent year-round E15 sales.

Farm and biofuel groups welcome move

The EPA’s proposed approach received support from agricultural and biofuel organisations.

Kurt Kovarik, vice president of federal affairs at Clean Fuels Alliance, said the action would help prevent another round of unaccounted-for refinery exemptions and the resulting loss of biofuel demand.

Corey McCray, vice president of government relations at the National Oilseed Processors Association, credited Nunn and other lawmakers for their efforts to maintain a strong RFS for farmers and soybean processors.

The Iowa Soybean Association also welcomed the proposal, with its Chief Officer of Advocacy and Demand Matt Herman urging the EPA to reallocate 100% of the lost volume.

John Deere also praised Nunn’s efforts, saying the proposed reallocation of RIN obligations could provide greater certainty for renewable fuel demand.

The EPA’s final decision on the supplemental rule will determine whether the exempted volumes are fully restored, a development closely watched by US ethanol producers, biodiesel manufacturers, farmers and agricultural processors.

text:
CUPERTINO, Calif., Sept. 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aemetis, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMTX), a diversified renewable natural gas and biofuels company, praised the unanimous passage of California Senate Bill 795, which will allow the state’s fuel retailers to utilize existing vapor recovery equipment to dispense E15 based on manufacturer certifications.

Using a 15% blend of ethanol would reduce the cost of blended gasoline to California consumers by $2.7 billion per year, according to a UC Berkeley study. E15 was approved for year-round use in California by Assembly Bill 30, which was signed into law in October 2025. However, the implementation of E15 has been delayed by equipment certification requirements, which SB 795 resolves.

“As a leading California ethanol producer for the past 15 years, Aemetis has long advocated for the state to allow E15 in order to lower the cost of gasoline and provide a choice for consumers,” said Eric McAfee, Chairman and CEO of Aemetis. “This regulatory fix is a major step in opening California’s market to more American-made ethanol.”

The use of E15 instead of E10 in California would add more than 600 million gallons of annual demand for ethanol, which is about 10 times the capacity of the Aemetis 65 million gallon per year ethanol plant in Keyes, California. In addition to ethanol, the Aemetis plant produces more than two million pounds per day of distillers grain that is supplied to about 80 dairies in the Central Valley to feed more than 100,000 dairy cows with high-value animal feed. The Aemetis plant is also the largest California producer of renewable CO2, which is captured and used in beverages and food processing.

“We are grateful for Governor Newsom and the State Legislature’s support of E15 as a choice to lower fuel costs for consumers and reduce pollution from on-road transportation,” added McAfee. “We look forward to continuing to work with California legislators and regulatory agencies to advance clean fuels in California, while driving down costs of food production in the state.”

SB 795 now awaits Governor Newsom’s signature.

title: Biofuels industry seeks policy stability to drive next phase of growth, says NITI Aayog adviser
description:

The government has also widened the feedstock base for ethanol and encouraged investment in distillery capacity.
National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories president Harshvardhan Patil said the industry currently faces an uncertain policy environment and called the ethanol scenario “dicey”.

text:
“Policy stability has to be there to give private investors the confidence to scale up existing and new biofuel production.”

The comments come as India’s ethanol blending programme has expanded rapidly over the past decade. Blending in petrol, which was less than 1.5 percent in 2013-14, reached 20 percent in 2025-26.

The programme, under which oil marketing companies blend domestically produced ethanol with petrol, aims to reduce crude oil imports while creating an additional market for agricultural produce. The government has also widened the feedstock base for ethanol and encouraged investment in distillery capacity.

National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories president Harshvardhan Patil said the industry currently faces an uncertain policy environment and called the ethanol scenario “dicey”.

“We are seeking that this green energy policy should be continued in a proper manner. Whatever decision the government takes, that has to be at least guided.”

Patil added that sudden decisions that make conditions harder for the industry should be reviewed.

A wider biofuel economy

Ram said the significance of biofuels extends beyond their use as a transport fuel, with the sector offering benefits in terms of energy security, decarbonisation and rural prosperity.

“Biofuels may not be viewed as merely a traditional fuel, but as a long-term pillar for India’s energy architecture.”

India’s transport sector consumes almost 20 percent of the country’s energy and accounts for around 10 percent of national greenhouse gas emissions, while remaining heavily dependent on imported fossil fuels, Ram said.

“Scaling domestic biofuels, particularly ethanol and compressed biofuels, where technology has matured, directly improves our trade balance and insulates us from global price volatility.”

However, Ram said the environmental benefits of biofuels depend on their feedstock and production pathways.

“Feedstock and production pathways matter particularly for the biofuels,” he said, pointing to compressed biogas (CBG) made from cattle dung, paddy straw and agricultural and vegetable waste.

“CBG produced from waste, like cattle dung, paddy straw, agri-vegetable waste, offers nearly net-zero emissions.”

Moving from the current blending success toward a broader bioeconomy would require greater feedstock diversification and stronger supply-chain infrastructure, Ram said.

This includes systems to collect, aggregate, store and transport agricultural residues and other biomass, which could otherwise remain an underutilised resource.

Also Read: Ethanol or a supply crunch? What’s behind the sudden rush in India’s sugar prices

New-age fuel

Patil said the E20 achievement should be treated as the beginning of the next phase rather than the end of the ethanol programme. “E20 should not be viewed as the end of the road. It should be viewed as the beginning of the next chapter.”

The industry’s next focus, he said, should be on diversification, greater efficiency and developing new applications for ethanol.

Second-generation (2G) ethanol, produced from agricultural residues rather than conventional sugar- and grain-based feedstocks, could help address crop-residue burning while creating additional income opportunities for farmers.

“Convert an agriculture residue disposal problem into an economic resource,” Patil suggested.

He also highlighted CBG as a way to connect waste management with energy production, giving examples of feedstocks such as cattle dung, agricultural residues, pressed mud, and municipal organic waste.

But the viability of CBG projects would depend on reliable feedstock supplies, biomass aggregation, assured demand, pipeline connectivity and commercially viable project economics, he said.

Patil also pointed to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) as a potential new market for the ethanol industry, saying technologies such as Alcohol-to-Jet could allow ethanol to be used as a feedstock for SAF.

The Brazil experience

Roberto Carlos Razera Papa, Agricultural Attache at the Embassy of Brazil, said Brazil’s ethanol programme was launched following the oil crisis of the 1970s, when the country was highly dependent on imported oil.

“What time taught us is that it was not only a solution to replace oil. It was much more.”

Brazil’s experience, he said, showed how an ethanol programme could evolve from an energy-security response into a wider agricultural and industrial ecosystem.

For India, the immediate challenge is to provide enough policy certainty to support investment while developing the feedstock, infrastructure and technology required to take the biofuel sector beyond petrol blending.

The order underscores the continuing importance of rail to Europe’s refined-products supply chain, particularly as oil companies and logistics operators seek reliable alternatives for moving fuels between refineries, storage facilities and distribution centres.

“The expansion of our fleet strengthens our long-term transportation capacity and supports the reliable supply of petroleum products to our customers,” said Jan Stephan, supply and marketing director at Rosneft Deutschland. “We are pleased to continue our successful partnership with GATX.”

text:
Saipem has secured an engineering services contract from Swiss renewable synthetic fuel producer Synhelion AG to advance the development of a commercial-scale synthetic fuel facility in Germany. The agreement covers pre-Front-End Engineering Design (pre-FEED) activities for the proposed plant, which will be established at RWE’s Chemiepark Knapsack industrial site in Hürth, Germany.

The planned facility is expected to have an annual production capacity of approximately 30,000 tonnes of RED-compliant renewable synthetic fuels. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) will represent the primary product, while the plant will also manufacture synthetic diesel and gasoline. These renewable fuels are intended to serve multiple transportation segments, including aviation, maritime shipping, and road mobility.

Under the contract, Saipem will prepare a comprehensive multidisciplinary pre-FEED engineering package. The work will focus on defining the plant’s overall configuration and integrating Synhelion’s proprietary synthetic fuel technology with fuel synthesis and upgrading processes. The engineering design will also incorporate the infrastructure available at RWE’s Chemiepark Knapsack site.

The pre-FEED phase represents an important step in the project’s development because it will establish the technical framework needed for subsequent stages. Saipem’s engineering package is expected to support the regulatory permitting process and provide the foundation for the future FEED phase. The work will ultimately contribute to preparations for the project’s Final Investment Decision (FID).

The collaboration strengthens Saipem’s position in the sustainable fuels sector, particularly in projects that require the integration of advanced technologies with large-scale industrial infrastructure. For Synhelion, the partnership provides engineering expertise to help translate its proprietary technology into a commercial-scale production facility.

The project also highlights the growing European focus on renewable fuels as the transportation sector seeks alternatives to conventional fossil-based fuels. SAF, in particular, is gaining importance as airlines and fuel producers face increasing pressure to reduce lifecycle carbon emissions and comply with tightening environmental regulations.

If successfully developed and commissioned, the facility could contribute to the expansion of Europe’s renewable synthetic fuel production capacity. It may also demonstrate the scalability of Synhelion’s technology while creating an additional source of low-carbon fuels for hard-to-abate transportation applications.

Overall, Saipem’s pre-FEED contract marks a significant development in the project pipeline and establishes an engineering pathway toward commercial-scale production of renewable synthetic fuels in Germany.

Product and Chemical Commodity Price Impact

The announcement is bullish for SAF and renewable synthetic fuel demand, as the proposed 30,000-tonne/year plant strengthens Europe’s emerging e-fuels capacity. However, the immediate impact on conventional chemical commodity prices should remain limited because the project is still at the pre-FEED stage and commercial production is several years away. In the longer term, higher SAF output could gradually reduce demand growth for conventional jet fuel, while renewable diesel and gasoline could compete with fossil-derived alternatives. Demand for hydrogen, carbon dioxide, catalysts, specialty chemicals, and renewable feedstocks may increase as synthetic fuel capacity expands, potentially supporting prices for these related commodities.

Axens S.A., a France-based technology provider specializing in sustainable refining, biofuels, and low-carbon solutions, has been selected by Canadian renewable fuel producer Expander Energy Inc. to supply its advanced Fischer-Tropsch (FT) Liquid Upgrading technology. The collaboration will support Expander Energy’s plans to develop sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel (RD) production capacity in Canada.

Axens’ technology will be integrated into Expander Energy’s patented Enhanced Biomass to Liquids (EBTL®) and Biomass Electrolysis to Liquids (BETL®) processes. This selection could provide Axens with opportunities to supply its technology across additional projects as Expander Energy expands its renewable fuels portfolio.

Tidewater Renewables Ltd. (TSX:LCFS) is a Canadian clean-fuels company focused on producing low-carbon fuels and advancing projects that support transportation decarbonisation. Its flagship renewable diesel and renewable hydrogen complex uses renewable feedstocks to produce lower-carbon alternatives to conventional transportation fuels.

Investor sentiment has improved considerably as operational reliability and Facility utilization have strengthened. The latest quarterly update demonstrated record operating performance, stronger margins and continued balance-sheet improvement, while management increased its outlook for the year.

Why Did Tidewater Renewables Ltd. (TSX:LCFS) Rise by 5.31% on 1 September, 2026?

Tidewater Renewables shares advanced 5.31% on September 1, extending the stock's strong recent momentum. Market trading data confirm the positive close and show that LCFS has appreciated substantially over longer recent periods as sentiment toward the company has recovered.

The latest advance appears to reflect continued investor reassessment following Tidewater Renewables' strong quarterly update rather than a major new company announcement on the session.

The central fundamental driver is improved performance at the renewable diesel and renewable hydrogen complex. Tidewater recently reported record average throughput at the facility, accompanied by record adjusted operating earnings. Management consequently increased its full-year guidance, signalling greater confidence in operating conditions for the remainder of the year.

The company has also continued reducing debt, supported by stronger operating margins and disciplined Capital allocation. This is important because balance-sheet improvement can reduce Financial Risk while increasing strategic flexibility.

The Business model of Tidewater Renewables Ltd.

Tidewater Renewables generates value through the production and sale of renewable fuels and associated environmental attributes. Its core facility processes renewable feedstocks including used cooking oil, animal fats and vegetable-based inputs to manufacture renewable diesel and renewable hydrogen.

The economics are supported not only by physical fuel sales but also by environmental credits created under Canadian and certain US low-carbon fuel programs. This gives the company exposure to both commodity markets and government-supported decarbonisation frameworks.

Co-location of the renewable diesel complex with existing refining infrastructure provides strategic advantages by allowing Tidewater Renewables to Leverage established facilities and reduce certain operating and infrastructure requirements.

Major Reasons Behind Upside

Record Operational Performance: The renewable diesel and renewable hydrogen complex recently achieved record average throughput, demonstrating improved reliability following earlier operational challenges.

Higher Management Outlook: Management raised its full-year expectations following stronger-than-anticipated operating performance and a constructive Margin environment.

Balance-Sheet Improvement: Continued debt reduction provides an important fundamental support for the Equity story by lowering financial leverage and improving flexibility.

Government Policy Support: Canada's clean-fuel policies and British Columbia's low-carbon fuel framework remain important structural supports for domestic renewable fuel production.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Opportunity: Tidewater has progressed its proposed sustainable aviation fuel project and recently entered a new initiative agreement with the British Columbia government providing additional low-carbon fuel credits. The development advances the project toward a potential final Investment decision.

Improving Renewable Fuel Economics: Better facility utilization allows fixed costs to be spread across greater production, potentially improving Operating Leverage when margins remain supportive.

Geopolitical tensions involving the US and Iran can indirectly benefit the strategic case for domestic and lower-carbon fuel Supply by increasing focus on energy security. However, they can also create Volatility in conventional energy prices, feedstock costs and financial markets. The impact on Tidewater Renewables is therefore mixed rather than uniformly positive.

What Are the Major Risks Investors Should Consider?

Execution risk: Maintaining reliable operations at high utilization remains essential.

Regulatory risk: Renewable fuel economics depend partly on environmental regulations and government incentive programs.

Funding risk: Major growth projects, particularly sustainable aviation fuel, could require substantial capital.

Market risk: Renewable fuel margins and environmental Credit values can fluctuate.

Competitive pressure: Additional renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel capacity could increase competition.

Operational challenges: Equipment failures or maintenance outages could materially affect production.

Economic uncertainty: Interest rates and broader economic conditions can influence financing and fuel demand.

Geopolitical exposure: Energy-market disruptions can affect commodity and feedstock economics.

Industry-specific risks: Feedstock availability, credit pricing and policy changes remain significant variables.

What Is the Dividend Outlook?

Tidewater Renewables currently does not present a dividend-oriented investment case. Available capital is being prioritised toward debt reduction, operational reliability and potential growth projects.

This strategy appears appropriate given the company's recent operational recovery. A stronger Balance Sheet could eventually expand shareholder-return options, but near-term capital allocation remains focused primarily on financial resilience and growth.

How Does Tidewater Renewables Ltd. Compare With Other Industry Peers?

Tidewater Renewables has a differentiated position among Canadian renewable fuel companies because it already operates commercial-scale renewable diesel infrastructure.

Its co-located facility provides potential cost advantages, while exposure to Canadian low-carbon fuel regulations creates access to environmental attributes alongside physical fuel revenues.

Compared with larger diversified energy companies, Tidewater Renewables has greater concentration risk. Performance depends heavily on its principal renewable fuel facility, making operational reliability particularly important.

However, that concentrated exposure can also provide greater sensitivity to improving renewable fuel economics and successful execution of future projects.

Sustained high facility utilization could support stronger operating cash generation.

Improving margins could reinforce the Earnings recovery.

Further debt reduction could lower financial risk.

Government clean-fuel incentives may support domestic renewable diesel economics.

Sustainable aviation fuel could create an important additional growth platform.

Stronger operational reliability could support a lasting valuation reassessment.

Bear Case:

Unexpected outages could interrupt the operational recovery.

Renewable fuel margins could weaken.

Environmental credit prices may become less supportive.

Policy changes could alter project economics.

Feedstock Inflation could pressure profitability.

Sustainable aviation fuel development could require significant capital and carry execution risk.

Volume Trends: Sustained participation would strengthen confirmation that the improving trend has broader market support.

Momentum Indicators: Momentum remains constructive following the latest advance, although the magnitude of the broader recovery increases the possibility of periodic consolidation.

Environmental considerations are central to Tidewater Renewables' investment proposition. Renewable diesel can materially reduce carbon intensity compared with conventional diesel, supporting transportation-sector decarbonisation.

The company's sustainable aviation fuel ambitions could further broaden its contribution to reducing transportation emissions if the project reaches commercial development.

Social considerations include employment, operational safety and relationships with communities surrounding its facilities.

From a governance perspective, disciplined capital allocation is especially important. Management's focus on debt reduction and controlled progression of major projects can help strengthen the investment case, although investors should continue monitoring leverage and project commitments.

Outlook

The outlook for Tidewater Renewables remains cautiously constructive. Operational performance has improved significantly, the renewable diesel complex is demonstrating stronger reliability and management has raised its expectations following a record quarter.

The company's balance-sheet trajectory is another important positive. Continued debt reduction can strengthen financial resilience and potentially improve future strategic flexibility.

Sustainable aviation fuel represents the next major source of optionality. Government support has advanced the project, although investors should wait for further clarity regarding financing, commercial arrangements and a final investment decision before assigning full value to the opportunity.

Overall, stronger operations, improved financial momentum and supportive clean-fuel policies underpin the positive sentiment around LCFS. Commodity volatility, regulatory dependence and operational concentration remain material risks, but continued execution could reinforce the company's improving fundamental profile.

Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Sunetra Pawar on Wednesday directed officials to immediately place before the state cabinet a proposal to introduce a soft loan scheme, on the lines of the Centre’s scheme, to help cooperative sugar factories prepare for the upcoming crushing season and ensure timely payment of the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) to sugarcane farmers.

Pawar issued the direction at a meeting held at Sahyadri State Guest House under her chairmanship to discuss the proposed soft loan policy and a policy for promoting by-products at cooperative sugar factories.

Highlighting the need to strengthen the financial capacity of sugar factories, Pawar said cooperative mills should reduce their dependence on sugar alone and focus on increasing revenue through the production of value-added by-products.

She suggested formulating a comprehensive policy to promote the various by-products and allied activities undertaken by cooperative sugar factories. Such a policy, she said, could help accelerate investments in solar energy, co-generation, first-generation (1G) ethanol, multi-feed ethanol, second-generation (2G) ethanol, compressed biogas (CBG), green hydrogen, bio-bitumen, biochemicals and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The report said the state Cooperation Department had prepared a proposal and sent it to the Finance Department, while the state government was expected to bear an estimated interest burden of around Rs 600 crore under the proposed package.

title: COMMENTARY: Why action lags ambition among States seeking SAF mandates

text:
The adoption and scale-up of sustainable aviation fuel remains one of the most intractable challenges in aviation decarbonisation. The International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) Long-Term Aspirational Goal (LTAG) projections suggest SAF could contribute up to 55% of required emissions reduction by 2050 under an optimistic scenario. In reality, production and adoption have tracked closer to the pessimistic forecast – a mere 15% contribution. Globally, meaningful uptake has occurred largely in the United States and Europe, both driven by aggressive public policy. Beyond these two poles, however, the picture is one of missed targets and diminished ambition. Underlying this are the real consequences of competitive disadvantages and administrative hurdles that face any smaller country or region seeking to follow suit, writes AirAsia’s Yap Mun Ching.

Consider the recent trajectory of national commitments: Japan, an early mover, had pledged a 10% SAF blend by 2030, only to slash this target to 1%. Singapore, which opened the world’s largest SAF refinery in 2023 and announced a levy from 2026, has since pushed implementation back by a year. Brazil has set a 1% SAF emissions reduction mandate from 2027, but without sufficient production capacity, it has to rely on an international book-and-claim system that is still evolving. South Korea, Thailand and Indonesia have also voiced intentions, but none has offered policy clarity.

Some reasons for the lag have been debated extensively. These include a broader shift in climate attitudes, challenges in scaling feedstock supply, slow commercialisation of emerging technologies, and the aviation industry’s protracted pandemic recovery compounded by new disruptions. This article does not revisit those arguments, nor does it seek to provide cover for inaction. Instead, it addresses a set of less discussed but equally consequential dilemmas facing airlines, airports and governments that, if left unaddressed, will continue to delay progress.

Designing the rulebook

For any country seeking to develop a SAF mandate, the most consequential hurdle is foundational: the policy itself must be designed from the ground up. This requires technical expertise spanning aviation operations, fuel production and climate accounting. At a minimum, this includes SAF accounting systems, emissions standards, certification guidelines, monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) procedures and incentive structures. For many smaller countries that lack existing climate legislation frameworks, the absence of a readily applicable template is a major impediment.

By contrast, CORSIA’s progress owed much to the fact that ICAO developed Annex 16, Volume IV as a detailed implementation framework which many countries could transpose directly into domestic law. The heavy lifting to draft, debate and develop was undertaken by experts in ICAO committees and disseminated through activities funded by the UN body and its donors. Without this institutional support, countries intending to move first often struggle to create rules from scratch.

Singapore’s SAF levy development illustrates this challenge. SAFCo, the designated entity, engaged multiple consultants to design and implement the levy mechanism, from SAF procurement and certification to matching SAF batches to levy charges and auditing collections. Yet, with less than a month left before going live, questions remain over how much SAF airlines will actually receive after administrative costs are deducted from the levy proceeds.

The unlevel playing field

Countries that do overcome design hurdles then have to contend with the inadvertent competitive disadvantage it would create for their aviation sectors and economies. This can be understood through three scenarios.

First, airlines in mandated countries will face an unlevel playing field on all routes where they compete directly with carriers from a non-mandated country, even if anti-tankering rules apply. Airlines based in non-mandated countries can spread cost increases on some routes across their entire networks while mandated competitors bear higher SAF costs on all outbound flights.

Second, in hub-and-spoke operations, the country that introduces a mandate on its main airport risks losing long-haul connectivity. Take this Southeast Asian example: if Bangkok introduces a 1% SAF mandate but Hanoi does not, a European carrier operating long-haul into the region would incur SAF costs on both outbound and inbound legs if hubbing in Bangkok but only outbound if hubbing in Hanoi. At today’s fuel prices, the cost difference would range between US$30 and US$40 per passenger. This risks creating traffic diversion, generating carbon leakage that undermines the mandate’s environmental objective.

Third, many developing countries operate on export-led development models. A higher-cost hub airport translates to reduced air connectivity and consequently, eroded investment attractiveness. Many also are heavily dependent on tourism. Higher travel costs affect incoming visitor numbers and cascade across the economy.

Without a global regime to mitigate these pressures and without funds to cushion the transitional impact, early movers have little recourse. Crucially, both EU and US policies contain financial provisions to reduce the SAF price differentials. These are generally absent in discussions of other SAF mandate proposals.

Furthermore, the proposed EU review of its Emissions Trading System (ETS) to extend coverage to flights within a 5,000km radius of Frankfurt explicitly aims to address the unlevel playing field that long-haul European carriers face against Gulf competitors. As a regional bloc, the EU has the ability to introduce regulation to neutralise the impact. This option is not available to smaller countries.

MRV nightmare

Another significant challenge lies in the administrative complexity that airlines would face. EU-based carriers need only to meet three MRV requirements to operate across 27 countries for CORSIA, ReFuelEU and EU ETS. By contrast, if just five of the 11 Southeast Asian countries introduce standalone mandates, an airline operating within the region could face at least seven distinct MRV regimes – one per mandated country, plus CORSIA and eventually one for domestic compliance frameworks.

Tracking the specific requirements for each scheme adds a further burden as no standard template or harmonised framework exists outside the EU. This is not an administrative quirk. Airlines that have trialled SAF batches for CORSIA eligibility report verification timelines of six to eight months per batch. While this timeline is expected to shorten over time, the prospect of certifying multiple batches purchased in multiple countries, each eligible for claims under different jurisdictions or for CORSIA, presents a daunting web of compliance complexity.

Global agreement vs regional and unilateral solutions

International or regional regimes are the obvious solutions to these challenges. CORSIA’s key benefit is its harmonised framework which applies in 130 countries and is set to expand when it enters its mandatory phase. Getting the world to move on SAF requires aligning biofuel blending targets, such as those adopted at the Third ICAO Conference on Aviation and Alternative Fuels (CAAF/3) in November 2023, with the existing CORSIA regime. However, ICAO processes are time-consuming. Even with broad agreement, global implementation would take years.

Less onerous would be for regional alignment to take place. Without a legislative body equivalent to the EU, regions such as ASEAN could coordinate among member states to agree on a common mandate design, quantum and implementation timelines. This would also require harmonisation of procedures, standards and mutual recognition of certifications. These could go a long way to level the regional playing field and reduce administrative overlaps.

In the absence of such progress, countries that seek to implement mandates must be prepared to provide transitional financing support. This requires elevating SAF implementation as a domestic priority and allocating budgetary resources to compensate for the loss of competitiveness until SAF production scales up sufficiently for market forces to function. The United Kingdom’s Revenue Guarantee Mechanism partially seeks to address the market failure around SAF with a levy on fuel suppliers, but without allocating taxpayer-funded support, the added cost falls squarely back on the aviation sector. The measure only targets lowering barriers to investment by producers. It does not address how to retain airline competitiveness against EU rivals who benefit from EU incentives or Gulf rivals not subject to any mandate.

Another mechanism open to countries whose objective is to grow a domestic production industry is to regulate prices and feedstock supplies. This is particularly relevant for countries such as China, Indonesia and Malaysia, which are currently net exporters of used cooking oil. Producer countries could first seek to limit feedstock exports, as China and Indonesia have done, reserving quantities required by domestic refineries and regulating SAF prices based on feedstock market rates and production costs. This would prevent producers from exercising monopolistic pricing linked to jet fuel movements and ensure that the countries’ objectives – to develop a SAF industry, spur domestic utilisation and shield against anti-competitive impact – are met.

From ambition to implementation

The SAF rollout will continue to be beleaguered by delays and paralysis unless serious attention can be given to these real world challenges. The gap between ambition and action is not merely a matter of political will or technological readiness. It is a function of policy design capacity, competitive asymmetry and administrative burden. They must be confronted directly as design parameters for effective policy.

Where global agreement is out of reach, the path forward could lie in regional coordination and harmonisation. This is where technical assistance can make a difference to close capacity gaps and where mutual recognition can spread roles and risks across several jurisdictions.

Countries that wish to demonstrate individual ambition and leadership must recognise that mandates alone cannot solve the SAF conundrum without addressing the ultimate question of who will pay and what trade-offs they are willing to accept. Certainly, progress is not absent around the globe. Several airlines – notably United Airlines, American Airlines, Air France-KLM Group and International Airlines Group – have signed binding offtake commitments. But these have not emerged in isolation – they are underpinned by domestic regulatory readiness, incentives and a travelling public willing to bear higher environmental costs. For the broader industry, the barriers remain substantial. Without addressing the gaps, the stakes will remain high for any country seeking to move first.

text:
A new direct air capture facility in New Jersey has begun operations, with the capacity to remove 450 tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere each year while producing about 475,000 gallons of clean water.

Developed by Avnos with funding from the U.S. Office of Naval Research, Project Brighton is located in Bridgewater and will support testing to use captured CO2 to produce sustainable aviation fuel, while also generating operational data for larger commercial deployments.

Capturing carbon and producing water together

Brighton is Avnos’ largest operating deployment to date and is located alongside the company’s Technology Development Center on Milltown Road.

The site combines research, testing and product development on one campus, allowing Avnos to validate its Hybrid Direct Air Capture, or HDAC, technology under real-world operating conditions as it prepares to scale the system.

Unlike some direct air capture technologies that require significant external heat or water inputs, Avnos says its HDAC process captures atmospheric CO2 while simultaneously producing clean water, without relying on external heat.

That combination is intended to make the technology suitable for applications ranging from data centers and geologic carbon storage to low-carbon fuel production.

“Brighton is our largest operating deployment to date and demonstrates our ability to deliver infrastructure at increasing scale,” said Will Kain, Founder and CEO of Avnos.

More from Energy

See All

“It also provides the operational experience and real-world performance data that will help accelerate future commercial deployments, while helping customers address interconnected energy, water and emissions challenges,” he added.

Captured CO2 could support aviation fuel production

One of Brighton’s key roles will be supporting Avnos’ work on converting carbon dioxide captured directly from the atmosphere into feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel.

Direct air capture removes CO2 already present in the atmosphere, after which the captured gas can either be permanently stored or used as an input for products such as synthetic fuels.

For the aviation sector, captured carbon could be combined with other inputs to produce fuels designed to reduce dependence on conventional fossil-based jet fuel.

Brighton’s development with funding from the Office of Naval Research also gives Avnos a larger operating platform for gathering performance data as it works toward commercial-scale deployments.

“Project Brighton reflects the kind of investment Somerset County, and New Jersey more broadly, works hard to attract – technology companies building real infrastructure at scale,” said Chris Edwards, President and CEO of Somerset County Business Partnership.

“Avnos has been part of our business community for several years now, and it’s great to see this project reach operational status,” he added.

Larger carbon capture project already in development

With Brighton operational, Avnos is also advancing Project Cedar, another HDAC deployment supported by up to $17 million in project financing.

Cedar is expected to use four HDAC modules designed around faster construction, greater scalability and more repeatable deployment, giving the company another step toward building direct air capture infrastructure at larger scales.

The company has also received backing from the U.S. Department of Energy and the U.S. Department of Defense as it develops HDAC systems for carbon removal, water production and other commercial applications.

title: China's SAF exports surge 70% in July, with Europe taking all shipments - BioEnergy Times
description:
China’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) exports rose sharply in July 2026, with almost the entire trade continuing to flow to Europe, highlighting the growing importance of the China-Europe SAF supply chain, ResourceWise reported.
From January to July, 99.97% of China’s SAF exports went to European markets, with only a marginal volume shipped elsewhere.
Belgium leads Chinese SAF imports Belgium was the largest destination for Chinese SAF in July, accounting for approximately 63% of exports.
Together, Belgium and the Netherlands took roughly 88.5% of China’s total SAF exports during the month.
